label: T:cont
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T:cont}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open with boundary of class $\mathcal{C}^1$\footnote{For the purpose of this work, it is enough to consider this case; however, the assumption about the $\mathcal{C}^1$ regularity of the boundary can be weakened. Likewise for Theorem \ref{T:comp}.}, $k\ge1$ integer, and $1\le p<\infty$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item If $kp<N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in\left[p,\frac{np}{n-kp}\right].
	\]
	\item If $kp=N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in[p,\infty[;
	\]
	If, moreover, $p=1$, then
	\[
	W^{N,1}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}(\Omega)\cap L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in[1,\infty].
	\]
	\item If $kp>N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}(\Omega)\cap L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in[p,\infty].
	\]
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: If $|\Omega|<\infty$, then the embeddings in Theorem \ref{T:cont} hold also for $q\in[1,p[$.

label: T:comp
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T:comp}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open and bounded with boundary of class $\mathcal{C}^1$, $k\ge1$ integer, and $1\le p<\infty$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item If $kp<N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in\biggl[1,\frac{np}{n-kp}\biggl[.
	\]
	\item If $kp=N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega) \quad \text{ for all } q\in[1,\infty[.
	\]
	\item If $kp>N$, then
	\[
	W^{k,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}(\overline\Omega).
	\]
\end{itemize}

Let $u_n\in\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}$ bounded. If $N\ge2$ or each $u_n$ is a nonincreasing function of $|x|$, then there exists $u\in\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}$ such that, up to a subsequence, $u_n\to u$ in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for every $p\in]2,2^*[$ (for every $p\in]2,\infty]$ if $N=1$).

title: Definition
body_md: Let $N,K,\nu\ge1$ integers and $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ open. A function $f\colon\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^K\to\mathbb{R}^\nu$ is called a \textit{Carath\'eodory function} if and only if it is continuous in $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$ for a.e. $x\in\Omega$ and measurable in $x\in\Omega$ for every $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
If there exists $C>0$ such that for a.e. $x\in\Omega$ and every $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$
\[
|f(x,u)|\le C(|u|^{p/r}+|u|^{q/s}),
\]
then $N_f\colon L^p(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^K)\cap L^q(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^K)\to L^r(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^\nu)+L^s(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^\nu)$ is continuous.

title: Example
body_md:
If $X$ is a Hilbert space with scalar product $(\cdot|\cdot)$, then the functional $\|\cdot\|^2\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^1$ and
\[
\left(\|\cdot\|^2\right)'(u)(v)=2(u|v) \quad \text{ for every } u,v\in X.
\]

label: T:diff
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T:diff}
Let $F\colon\mathbb{R}^N\times\mathbb{R}^K\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable in $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$ and such that $\nabla_uF\colon\mathbb{R}^N\times\mathbb{R}^K\to\mathbb{R}^K$ is a Carath\'eodory function. If there exists $C_1>0$ and, if $N\in\{1,2\}$, $p\ge2$ such that for a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and every $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$
\[
|\nabla_uF(x,u)|\le C_1(|u|+|u|^{2^*-1}) \quad \text{ if } N\ge3
\]
or
\[
|\nabla_uF(x,u)|\le C_1(|u|+|u|^{p-1}) \quad \text{ if } N\in\{1,2\},
\]
then $I\colonH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K\to\mathbb{R}$ defined as
\[
I(u):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F\bigl(x,u(x)\bigr)\,dx
\]
is of class $\mathcal{C}^1$ and
\[
I'(u)(v)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla_uF\bigl(x,u(x)\bigr)\cdot v(x)\,dx \quad \text{ for every } u,v\inH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K.
\]
If, moreover, $N\ge3$ and there exists $C_2>0$ such that for a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and every $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$
\[
|\nabla_uF(x,u)|\le C_2|u|^{2^*-1},
\]
then $I\colon\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K\to\mathbb{R}$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^1$ and
\[
I'(u)(v)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla_uF\bigl(x,u(x)\bigr)\cdot v(x)\,dx \quad \text{ for every } u,v\in\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K.
\]

label: T:Palais
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T:Palais}
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space, $\mathcal{G}$ a topological group acting isometrically on $\mathcal{H}$, and $J\in\mathcal{C}^1(\mathcal{H})$ such that $J(gx)=J(x)$ for every $g\in\mathcal{G}$ and $x\in\mathcal{H}$. Define $\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{G}:=\Set{x\in\mathcal{H}|gx=x \text{ for all } g\in\mathcal{G}}$. If $x\in\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{G}$ is a critical point of $J|_{\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{G}}$, then it is a critical point of $J$.

	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u^*|^2\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2\,dx.

title: Lemma
body_md: $L^\Phi=L^\Phi(\mathbb{R}^3)^3$ and their norms are equivalent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\mathbf{U}\in L^\Phi(\mathbb{R}^3)^3$ we use the norm $|\mathbf{U}|_{\Phi,3}:=\max_{i\in\{1,2,3\}}|\mathbf{U}_i|_\Phi$, with $\mathbf{U}=(\mathbf{U}_1,\mathbf{U}_2,\mathbf{U}_3)$. Since $\Phi$ is increasing on positive numbers, for every $k>0$
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi\left(\frac{|\mathbf{U}_i|}k\right)dx \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi\left(\frac{|\mathbf{U}|}k\right)dx,
\]
hence, if the second integral is less than $1$, so is the first one. Taking the infimum over $k>0$ we obtain $|\mathbf{U}_i|_\Phi\le|\mathbf{U}|_\Phi$ for every $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $|\mathbf{U}|_{\Phi,3}\le|\mathbf{U}|_\Phi$. In particular, $L^\Phi(\mathbb{R}^3)^3\subset L^\Phi$.

On the other hand, since $\Phi$ is convex,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi\left(\frac{|\mathbf{U}|}{k}\right)dx \le \frac13\sum_{i=1}^3 \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi\left(\frac{3|\mathbf{U}_i|}{k}\right)dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi\left(\frac{3\max_{i=1,2,3}|\mathbf{U}_i|}{k}\right)\,dx,
\]
so $|\mathbf{U}|_\Phi \le 3\max_{i=1,2,3}|\mathbf{U}_i|_\Phi = 3|\mathbf{U}|_{\Phi,3}$ and, in particular, $L^\Phi\subset L^\Phi(\mathbb{R}^3)^3$.

label: L:Hel
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $w\in\mathcal{W}$ and $\varphi_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ such that $|w -\nabla\varphi_n|_{\Phi}\to 0$.
Then for every $\psi\in\mathcal{C}_c^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}w\cdot\nabla\times\psi\,dx
=\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\nabla \varphi_n\cdot\nabla\times\psi\,dx=
\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\nabla\times(\nabla \varphi_n)\cdot\psi\,dx=0
\]
where we have used Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(ii)} and the fact that $\nabla\times\psi \in L^\Psi$. Hence $\nabla\times w=0$ in the sense of distributions and
$\|w\|_{\textup{curl},\Phi}=|w|_{\Phi}$. Therefore $\mathcal{W}$ is closed in $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$; moreover, it is easily checked that $\mathcal{V}$ is closed in $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$.

Now, take any $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$ and $\varphi_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ such that $\varphi_n\to\mathbf{U}$ in $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$. Let $\varphi_n^2\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ be the Newtonian potential of $\nabla\cdot\varphi_n$, i.e., $\varphi_n^2$ solves $\Delta \varphi_n^2 = \nabla\cdot\varphi_n$. Note that the derivative $\partial_i\varphi_n^2$ is the Newtonian potential of $\nabla\cdot\partial_i\varphi_n$. Since $\varphi_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, then by \cite[Proposition 1]{Iwaniec}, $\nabla\varphi_n^2$ and $ \nabla(\partial_i\varphi_n^2) \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ for every $r\in\,]1,\infty[$. Hence from Lemma \ref{L:emb}
\[
\nabla \varphi_n^2\in L^6(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)\subset L^{\Phi}
\] 
and $\varphi_n^1:=\varphi_n-\nabla \varphi_n^2\in L^{\Phi}$. Moreover, $\varphi_n^1,\partial_i\varphi_n^1\in L^r(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$.
We also have $\nabla\times\varphi_n^1 = \nabla\times\varphi_n$  and $\nabla\cdot\varphi_n^1=0$ pointwise. Using these two equalities and integrating by parts we obtain
$|\nabla\varphi^1_n|_2 = |\nabla\times\varphi^1_n|_2 = |\nabla\times\varphi_n|_2$. It follows that for every $m,n$
\[
|\nabla(\varphi_n^1-\varphi_m^1)|_{2}=|\nabla\times(\varphi_n^1-\varphi_m^1)|_{2}=|\nabla\times(\varphi_n-\varphi_m)|_{2}\leq \|\varphi_n-\varphi_m\|_{\textup{curl},\Phi},
\]
thus $\varphi_n^1$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{D}$. Let $v:=\lim_n\varphi_n^1$ in $\mathcal{D}$. Then
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}v\cdot\nabla \varphi\,dx=\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\varphi^1_n\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0
\]
for every $\varphi\in\mathcal{C}_c^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, hence $\nabla\cdot v=0$ and $v\in\mathcal{V}$.
Moreover,
\[
|\nabla\times(\varphi_n^1-v)|_{2}=|\nabla(\varphi_n^1-v)|_{2}\to 0,
\]
so $\varphi_n^1\to v$ in  $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$ and
$\nabla \varphi^2_n=\varphi_n-\varphi^1_n\to\mathbf{U}-v$ in $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$. Since $\mathcal{W}$ is closed in $\mathcal{D}(\textup{curl},\Phi)$, then $\mathbf{U}-v\in \mathcal{W}$ and we get the decomposition
$$\mathbf{U}=v+(\mathbf{U}-v)\in\mathcal{V}+\mathcal{W}.$$

Now take $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{V}\cap\mathcal{W}$. Then $\nabla\times\mathbf{U}=0$, so by \cite[Lemma 1.1 \textit{(i)}]{Leinfelder}, $\mathbf{U}=\nabla\xi$ for some $\xi\in W^{1,6}_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Since $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{U}=0$, $\xi$ is harmonic and therefore so is $\mathbf{U}$. Hence 
\[
0 = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\mathbf{U}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{U}\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|\nabla\mathbf{U}|^2\,dx
\] 
and so $\mathbf{U}=0$, thus  $\mathcal{V}\cap\mathcal{W}=\{0\}$ and we obtain \eqref{e-Hel}.

The equivalence of norms follows from Lemma \ref{L:emb}.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P:classC1}
$J\in\mathcal{C}^1(\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W})$ and
\[
J'(v,w)(v',w')=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\nabla v\cdot\nabla v'-f(x,v+w)\cdot(v'+w')\,dx
\]

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From Lemma \ref{L:emb}, the proof is complete if we prove that $I\in\mathcal{C}^1(L^\Phi)$, where $I(\mathbf{U}) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})\,dx$, and $I'(\mathbf{U})(\mathbf{V})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{V}\,dx$ for every $\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in L^\Phi$. Let $\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in L^\Phi$ and $t\ne0$ (we can assume $|t|\le1$). Then
\[\begin{split}
\frac{I(\mathbf{U})-I(\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{V})}{t} & =\frac1t\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})-F(x,\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{V})\,dx\\
& =\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,\mathbf{U}+\theta t\mathbf{V})\cdot\mathbf{V}\,dx
\end{split}\]
for some $\theta=\theta(t)\in[0,1]$. Since $f$ is a Charat\'eodory function, for a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$
\[
\lim_{t\to0}f\bigl(x,\mathbf{U}(x)+\theta t\mathbf{V}(x)\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{V}(x)=f\bigl(x,\mathbf{U}(x)\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{V}(x).
\]
Moreover, from (F3) and the monotonicity of $\Phi'$,
\[
|f(x,\mathbf{U}+\theta t\mathbf{V})\cdot\mathbf{V}| \le c_1\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}+\theta t\mathbf{V}|)|\mathbf{V}| \le c_1\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}|+|\mathbf{V}|)|\mathbf{V}| \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^3)
\]
owing to Lemmas \ref{L:all} \textit{(ii)} and \ref{L:forC1}. In view of the dominated convergence theorem, $I'(\mathbf{U})(\mathbf{V})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{V}\,dx$. In addition, the same argument proves that, for a fixed $\mathbf{U}\in L^\Phi$, the linear map
\[
\mathbf{V}\in L^\Phi\mapsto I'(\mathbf{U})(\mathbf{V})\in\mathbb{R}
\]
is continuous. Now we prove that $I'\in \mathcal{C}(L^\Phi,L^\Psi)$ (recall that $L^\Psi\simeq(L^\Phi)'$). Let $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ in $L^\Phi$. We want to prove that $\lim_n|f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_n)-f(\cdot,\mathbf{U})|_\Psi=0$, or equivalently
\[
\lim_n\left|\frac{f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_n)-f(\cdot,\mathbf{U})}{2c_1}\right|_\Psi=0,
\]
where $c_1$ is the same as (F3). In view of Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iii)}, this is the same as proving that
\[
\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Psi\left(\left|\frac{f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_n)-f(\cdot,\mathbf{U})}{2c_1}\right|\right)\,dx=0.
\]
By the same classical argument used for Lebesgue spaces (see, e.g., \cite[Proof of Theorem 3.11]{Rudin}) together with Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iv)}, $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$ up to a subsequence, hence $\Psi\bigl(|f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_n)-f(x,\mathbf{U})|/(2c_1)\bigr)\to0$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$. With the intent to use again the dominated convergence theorem, from (F3), Lemma \ref{L:forC1}, and the convexity of $\Psi$ we have
\[\begin{split}
\Psi\left(\left|\frac{f(x,\mathbf{U}_n)-f(x,\mathbf{U})}{2c_1}\right|\right) & \le \Psi\left(\frac{\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}_n|)+\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}|)}2\right)\\
& \le \frac{\Psi\bigl(\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}_n|)\bigr)+\Psi\bigl(\Phi'(|\mathbf{U}|)\bigr)}2\\
& \le \frac{\Phi(|\mathbf{U}_n|)+\Phi(|\mathbf{U}|)}2
\end{split}\]
and
\[
\Phi(|\mathbf{U}_n|)\le\frac{\Phi(2|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|)}2+\frac{\Phi(2|\mathbf{U}|)}2.
\]
Finally, since $\Phi(2|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|)\to0$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$, from \cite[Lemma A.1]{Willem} there exists $g\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$ such that $\Phi(2|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|)\le g$ for every $n$.

label: L:flow
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:flow}
	Suppose $(M)_0^\beta$ holds for some $\beta>0$ and let $u \in \mathcal{J}_0^\beta\setminus \mathcal{K}$. Then either $\lim_{t \to T(u)^-}\eta(t,u)$ exists and belongs to $\mathcal{K}$ or $\lim_{t\to T(u)^-}\mathcal{J}(\eta(t,u)) = -\infty$. In the latter case, $T(u)=\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $T(u)<\infty$ and let $0\le s<t<T(u)$. Then
	\[
	\|\eta(t,u)-\eta(s,u)\| \le \int_s^t \left\|V\bigl(\eta(\tau,u)\bigr)\right\|\,d\tau \le t-s.
	\] 
	Hence the limit exists and, if it were not a critical point, then $\eta(\cdot,u)$ could be extended for $t>T(u)$.
	
	Suppose now $T(u)=\infty$ and $\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(\cdot,u)\bigr)$ is bounded from below. We distinguish three cases: 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(i)] $t\mapsto \eta(t,u)$ is bounded,
		\item[(ii)] $t\mapsto \eta(t,u)$ is unbounded but $\|\eta(t,u)\|\not\to\infty$,
		\item[(iii)] $\|\eta(t,u)\|\to\infty$.
	\end{itemize} 
	(i) We follow an argument in \cite{SzWe}. We will show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $t_\varepsilon>0$ such that
	$\|\eta(t_\varepsilon,u)-\eta(t,u)\|<\varepsilon$ for all $t \ge t_\varepsilon$ (this implies $\lim_{t \to \infty}\eta(t,u)$ exists and so, as before, it is a critical point). Arguing by contradiction, we can find $\varepsilon\in\,]0,m_0^\beta/2[$, $R>0$ and $t_n\to\infty$ such that $\|\eta(t_n,u)\|\le R$ and $\|\eta(t_n,u)-\eta(t_{n+1},u)\| = \varepsilon$ for all $n$.  Let $t_n^1$ be the smallest $t\in\,]t_n,t_{n+1}[$ such that $\|\eta(t_n,u)-\eta(t_n^1,u)\|= \varepsilon/3$ and $t_n^2$ the largest $t\in\,]t_n^1,t_{n+1}[$ such that $\|\eta(t_{n+1},u)-\eta(t_n^2,u)\|= \varepsilon/3$. Set $\kappa_n := \min \Set{\lVert\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\rVert|t\in[t_n,t_n^1]}>0$. Then
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\frac{\varepsilon}3 & = \|\eta(t_n^1,u)-\eta(t_n,u)\| \le \int_{t_{n}}^{t_n^1}  \big\|V\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\big\| \,dt \le t_n^1-t_n \\ 
		& \le \frac{2}{\kappa_n} \int_{t_n}^{t_n^1} \mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\bigl(V\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\bigr)\,dt = \frac2{\kappa_n}\Bigl(\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n,u)\bigr)-\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n^1,u)\bigr)\Bigr).
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	Since $\mathcal{J}(\eta(t_n,u))-\mathcal{J}(\eta(t_n^1,u))\to 0$, also $\kappa_n\to 0$, hence we can choose $s_n^1\in[t_n,t_n^1]$ such that, if $u_n:= \eta(s_n^1,u)$, then $\mathcal{J}'(u_n)\to 0$. Since  $\|\eta(s_n^1,u)\|$ is bounded, $u_n$ is a Cerami sequence. A similar argument shows the existence of $v_n:= \eta(s_n^2,u)$, $s_n^2\in[t_n^2,t_{n+1}]$, such that $\mathcal{J}'(v_n)\to 0$. Hence
	\[
	\frac\varepsilon 3 \le \liminf_n\|u_n-v_n\|\le \limsup_n\|u_n-v_n\|\le\varepsilon +\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon<m_0^\beta,
	\]
	a contradiction to $(M)_0^\beta (b)$.
	
	(ii) Observe that there are no Cerami sequences in $X^+\setminus\overline B_{M_0^\beta}$ at any level $\alpha\in[0, \beta]$ according to $(M)_0^\beta (a)$. Since $\eta(t,u)$ is unbounded but $\|\eta(t,u)\|\not\to\infty$, there exists $R>M_0^\beta$ such that $\eta(t,u)\in B_R$ for arbitrarily large $t>0$. Then we can find $t_n, t_n^1$ so that $t_n\to\infty$, $\|\eta(t_n,u)\| = R+1$ and $t_n^1$ is the smallest $t>t_n$ with $\|\eta(t,u)\| = R$. We can also assume that $\|\eta(s,u)\|\leq R+1$ for $s\in [t_n,t_n^1]$. Let $\kappa_n$ be as above. Then
	\[
	1\le \|\eta(t_n^1,u)-\eta(t_n,u)\| \le \frac2{\kappa_n}\Bigl(\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n,u)\bigr)-\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n^1,u)\bigr)\Bigr)
	\]
	and hence $\kappa_n\to 0$. So we see that there exists $u_n:= \eta(s_n^1,u)$, $s_n^1\in[t_n,t_n^1]$, such that  $R\le \|u_n\|\le R+1$ and $\mathcal{J}'(u_n)\to 0$. Thus we have found a Cerami sequence in $X^+\setminus\overline{B}(0,M_0^\beta)$ which is impossible. This shows that case (ii) can never occur.
	
	(iii) There exist $R_0>0$ and $\delta>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{J}'(v)\|\ge \delta/\|v\|$ whenever $\|v\|\ge R_0$ and $v\in \mathcal{J}_0^\beta$, because otherwise there exists an unbounded Cerami sequence. Choose $t_0>0$ so that $\|\eta(t,u)\|\ge R_0$ and $\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_0,u)\bigr)-\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr) \le \delta/8$ for $t\ge t_0$. For $n\gg1$ let $t_n\ge t_0$ be the smallest $t$ such that $\|\eta(t,u)\|=n$ and let $\kappa_n := \min\Set{\lVert\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\rVert|t\in[t_0,t_n]}$. From the choice of $t_n$,
	\[
	\kappa_n \ge \min_{t\in [t_0,t_n]} \frac{\delta}{\|\eta(t,u)\|} = \frac{\delta}{\|\eta(t_n,u)\|}.
	\]
	It follows from the same argument as above that for $n\gg1$
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\frac12 \|\eta(t_n,u)\| & \le \|\eta(t_n,u)-\eta(t_0,u)\| \le \frac2{\kappa_n}\Bigl(\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_0,u)\bigr)-\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n,u)\bigr)\Bigr) \\
		& \le \frac{2}{\delta}\|\eta(t_n,u)\|\Bigl(\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_0,u)\bigr)-\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t_n,u)\bigr)\Bigr)\le\frac14\|\eta(t_n,u)\|.
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	This is a contradiction and hence also case (iii) can be ruled out.

title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(i)} It follows immediately from the properties of the Krasnosel'skii genus.
	
	\textit{(ii)} For every $h\in\mathcal{H}$
	\[\begin{split}
	i^*(A\cup B) & \le \gamma\bigl(h(A\cup B)\cap S_r\bigr) = \gamma\Bigl(\bigl(h(A)\cup h(B)\bigr)\cap S_r\Bigr)\\
	& \le \gamma\bigl(h(A)\cap S_r\bigr) + \gamma\bigl(h(B)\bigr) = \gamma\bigl(h(A)\cap S_r\bigr) + \gamma(B)
	\end{split}\]
	where in the last equality we used that $h$ is a homeomorphism. Taking the minimum over all $h\in\mathcal{H}$ on the right-hand side we obtain the conclusion.
	
	\textit{(iii)} Since $\mathcal{J}\bigl(g(u)\bigr)\le\mathcal{J}(u)$ for all $u\in X^+$, $h\circ g\in\mathcal{H}$ if $h\in\mathcal{H}$. Hence $\Set{h\circ g|h\in\mathcal{H}}\subset \mathcal{H}$ and therefore
	\[
	\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\gamma\bigl(h(A)\cap S_r\bigr) \le \min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\gamma\bigl((h\circ g)(A)\cap S_r\bigr).
	\]
	
	\textit{(iv)} Since the statement is obviously true for $k=0$, we can assume that $k\ge1$. From Lemma \ref{L:infty}, $\mathcal{J}(u)<0$ on $X_k\setminus B_R$ if $R$ is sufficiently large. Let $D := X_k\cap\overline B_R$. Suppose by contradiction that $i^*(D)<k$ and choose $h\in\mathcal{H}$ such that $\gamma\bigl(h(D)\cap S_r\bigr)<k$.
	
	If $k=1$, then $\gamma\bigl(h(D)\cap S_r\bigr)=0$, i.e., $h(D)\cap S_r=\emptyset$. Therefore either $\|h(u)\|<r$ for every $u\in D$ or $\|h(u)\|>r$ for every $u\in D$. Since $h(0)=0$, the latter is ruled out. If $u\in\partial D=X_k\cap S_R$, recalling that $\mathcal{J}(v)\ge 0$ for every $v\in B_r$, we then have $0\le\mathcal{J}\bigl(h(u)\bigr)\le\mathcal{J}(u)<0$, a contradiction.
	
	If $k\ge2$, fix an odd mapping 
	$$f\colon h(D)\cap S_r\to \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\setminus\{0\}.$$ 
	Let $U:= h^{-1}(B_r\cap X^+)\cap X_k$. There follows that $U\subset D\setminus\partial D$ and hence $U$ is an open and bounded neighbourhood of 0 in $X_k$. If $u\in \partial U$, then $h(u)\in S_r$ and therefore $f\circ h|_{\partial U}\colon \partial U \to \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\setminus\{0\}$, contradicting the Borsuk-Ulam theorem \cite[Proposition II.5.2]{Struwe}, \cite[Theorem D.17]{Willem}.

label: e-entrancetime1
title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(a)} Suppose that $\mathcal{J}$ does not have any critical values in $[c_{\mathcal{M}},c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0]$ for some $\varepsilon_0\in\,]0,\varepsilon]$. Thus $\mathcal{J}$ has only the trivial critical point 0 in $\mathcal{J}^{c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0}$.
	Take $u\in\mathcal{J}^{c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0}$ and
	observe that, from Lemma \ref{L:flow}, either $\lim_{t \to T(u)^-}\eta(t,u)=0$ or $\lim_{t\to T(u)^-}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr) = -\infty$. 
	Hence we may define the entrance time map $e:\mathcal{J}^{c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0}\to [0,\infty[$ by the formula
	\[
	e(u):=\inf\Set{t\in [0,T(u)[|  \mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\leq c_{\mathcal{M}}/2}.
	\]
	Let us prove that $e$ is continuous. Take $u_n,\bar u\in\mathcal{J}^{c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0}$ such that $u_n\to\bar u$: if by contradiction $e(u_n)\to\infty$ up to a subsequence, then, recalling that $\mathcal{J}$ is decreasing along the trajectories of $\eta$ and fixing $t\in]e(\bar{u}),T(\bar{u})[$,
	\[\begin{split}
	\frac{c_{\mathcal{M}}}{2} & = \lim_n\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta\bigl(e(u_n),u_n\bigr)\bigr) \le \lim_n\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u_n)\bigr)\\
	& = \mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,\bar{u})\bigr) < \mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta\bigl(e(u),u\bigr)\bigr) = \frac{c_{\mathcal{M}}}{2};
	\end{split}\]
	therefore $e(u_n)\to t$ up to a subsequence for some $t\ge0$ and so
	\[
	\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,\bar u)\bigr) = \lim_n\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta\bigl(e(u_n),u_n\bigr)\bigr) = \frac{c_{\mathcal{M}}}{2} = \mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta\bigl(e(\bar u),\bar u\bigr)\bigr),
	\]
	i.e., $t=e(\bar u)$. Now take any $\sigma\in\Sigma$ such that 
	\[
	\mathcal{J}\bigl(\sigma(t)\bigr)<c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0 \quad \text{for all } t\in[0,1],
	\]
	where $\Sigma$ is given by \eqref{e-Gamma_Phi}. Since $e$ is continuous,
	$\tilde{\sigma}(t):=\eta\big(e\bigl(\sigma(t)\bigr),\sigma(t)\big)$ is a continuous path in $X^+$ such that $\mathcal{J}\bigl(\tilde{\sigma}(1)\bigr)\leq \mathcal{J}\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)<0$. Hence $\tilde{\sigma}\in\Sigma$ and
	\[
	c_{\mathcal{M}}=\inf_{\sigma'\in\Sigma}\sup_{t\in [0,1]}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\sigma'(t)\bigr)\leq \sup_{t\in [0,1]}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\tilde{\sigma}(t)\bigr)\leq c_{\mathcal{M}}/2.
	\]
	The obtained contradiction proves that either $c_{\mathcal{M}}$ is a critical value or for every $\varepsilon_0\in\,]0,\varepsilon]$ there exists a critical value in $]c_{\mathcal{M}},c_{\mathcal{M}}+\varepsilon_0]$.
	
	\textit{(b)} Take $\beta\geq a$ and let
	\begin{equation*}
		\mathcal{K}^\beta:=\Set{u\in\mathcal{K}|\mathcal{J}(u)=\beta}.
	\end{equation*}
	Since there are finitely many critical orbits, there exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that
	\begin{equation*}              
	\mathcal{K}\cap \mathcal{J}_{\beta-\varepsilon_0}^{\beta+\varepsilon_0}=\mathcal{K}^\beta.
	\end{equation*} 
	In view of Lemma \ref{L:discrete}, there exists $\delta\in \,]0,m_0^{\beta+\varepsilon_0}[$ such that $\overline B(u,\delta)\cap \overline B(v,\delta) = \emptyset$ for every $u,v\in\mathcal{K}^\beta$, $u\ne v$. We show that there exists $\varepsilon\in\,]0,\varepsilon_0[$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-entrancetime1}
	\lim_{t\to T(u)^-}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr) < \beta -\varepsilon \quad\hbox{for every } u\in \mathcal{J}^{\beta+\varepsilon}_{\beta-\varepsilon}\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta).
	\end{equation}
	We assume $\mathcal{K}^\beta\ne\emptyset$, the other case being trivial.
	                                                                                                                                                                                                    
	          
	Consider the set
	\[
	A_0:=\Set{u\in \mathcal{J}^{\beta+\varepsilon_0}_{\beta-\varepsilon_0}\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)| \lim_{t \to T(u)^-}\eta(t,u)\in \mathcal{K}^\beta}.
	\]
	For every $u\in A_0$ we define
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		t_0(u)&:=\inf\Set{t\in [0,T(u)[|  \eta(s,u)\in B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\hbox{ for all }s> t},\\
		t(u)&:=\inf\Set{t\in [t_0(u),T(u)[|  \eta(t,u)\in B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta/2)}
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	and note that $0\leq t_0(u)< t(u)<T(u)$. There holds
	\begin{equation}\label{e-t}
	\begin{split}
	\frac{\delta}{2} & \leq
	\big\|\eta\bigl(t_0(u),u\bigr)-\eta\bigl(t(u),u\bigr)\big\|  \leq \int_{t_0(u)}^{t(u)}\big\|V\bigl(\eta(s,u)\bigr)\big\|\, ds\\
	& \leq t(u)-t_0(u). 
	\end{split}\end{equation}
	Let
	$$\rho:=\inf\Set{\big\lVert\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\big\rVert | u\in A_0,\ t\in[t_0(u),t(u)]}.$$
	If $\rho=0$ then we find $u_n\in A_0 $ and $t_n\in\,]t_0(u_n),t(u_n)[$ such that $$\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(t_n,u_n)\bigr)\to 0 \hbox{ as } n\to\infty.$$
	Since $t_n> t_0(u_n)$, we have $\eta(t_n,u_n)\in B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)$ and passing to a subsequence we can find $u_0\in\mathcal{K}^\beta$ and $g_n\in G$ such that
	$$g_n\eta(t_n,u_n)\in B(u_0,\delta).$$ Since $t_n<t(u_n)$, we see that
	$$g_{n}\eta(t_n,u_n)\notin B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta/2).$$
	Let $w_n:=u_0$, $v_n:=g_n\eta(t_n,u_n)$. Then $w_n$ and $v_n$ are two Cerami sequences such that $\delta/2 \le \|v_n-w_n\| \le \delta<m_0^{\beta+\varepsilon_0}$, a contradiction.
	Therefore $\rho>0$ and we take 
	$$\varepsilon < \min\Big\{\varepsilon_0,\frac{\delta\rho}8\Big\}.$$ 
	Now let $u\in \mathcal{J}_{\beta-\varepsilon}^{\beta+\varepsilon}\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)$ and suppose by contradiction that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-contrA0}
	\lim_{t\to T(u)^-}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)\ge\beta-\varepsilon,
	\end{equation}
	which owing to Lemma \ref{L:flow} yields $\lim_{t \to T(u)^-}\eta(t,u)\in\mathcal{K}^\beta$, i.e., $u\in A_0$. Since
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\mathcal{J}\Bigl(\eta\bigl(t(u),u\bigr)\Bigr)-\mathcal{J}\Bigl(\eta\bigl(t_0(u),u\bigr)\Bigr) & =-\int_{t_0(u)}^{t(u)}\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(s,u)\bigr)\Bigl(V\bigl(\eta(s,u)\bigl)\Bigr)\,ds\\
		& \leq -\frac12\int_{t_0(u)}^{t(u)}\big\|\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(s,u)\bigr)\big\|\, ds,
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	we obtain using \eqref{e-t}
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\lim_{t\to T(u)^-}\mathcal{J}\bigl(\eta(t,u)\bigr)&\leq \mathcal{J}\Bigl(\eta\bigl(t(u),u\bigr)\Bigr)
		\leq\beta +\varepsilon -\frac12\int_{t_0(u)}^{t(u)}\big\|\mathcal{J}'\bigl(\eta(s,u)\bigr)\big\|\, ds\\
		&\leq \beta+\varepsilon -\frac{\delta\rho}4 < \beta-\varepsilon.
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	This contradicts \eqref{e-contrA0}, hence \eqref{e-entrancetime1} holds.
	                                                                                                                                                                                  
	
	Define 
	\[
	\beta_k :=  \inf_{A\in\mathcal{A},\,i^*(A)\ge k} \max_{u\in A}\mathcal{J}(u), \quad k=1,2,\dots
	\]
	and note that from Lemma \ref{L:index} all the $\beta_k$ are well defined, finite, and $a\le\beta_1\le\beta_2\le\dots$.
	Let $\beta=\beta_k$  for some $k\geq 1$. If the set $\mathcal{K}^\beta$ is nonempty, then it is discrete and we can order its elements in pairs $\pm u_j$ and let the map $\phi\colon\mathcal{K}^\beta\to\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ be given by $\phi(\pm u_j)=\pm 1$. From the choice of $\delta$ we can extend $\phi$ to $\overline B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)$, whence
	$$\gamma\bigl(\overline B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\bigr)=\gamma (\mathcal{K}^\beta)\le1.$$
	Choose $\varepsilon>0$ such that \eqref{e-entrancetime1} holds. 
	Take Lipschitz continuous cutoff functions $\chi,\xi$ such that $\chi=0$ in $B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta/4)$, $\chi=1$ in $X^+\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta/2)$, $\xi=1$ in $\mathcal{J}_{\beta-\varepsilon}^{\beta+\varepsilon}$, and $\xi=0$ in $X^+\setminus U$ , where $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $\mathcal{J}_{\beta-\varepsilon}^{\beta+\varepsilon}$ with $\mathcal{K}\cap U=\mathcal{K}^\beta$.
	Let
	$\widetilde\eta:\mathbb{R}\times X^+\to  X^+$ be the flow given by
	\begin{equation*}
	\left\{
	\begin{aligned}
	&\partial_t \widetilde\eta(t,u)=-\chi\bigl(\widetilde\eta(t,u)\bigr)\xi\bigl(\widetilde\eta(t,u)\bigr) V\bigl(\widetilde\eta(t,u)\bigr)\\
	&\widetilde\eta(0,u)=u.
	\end{aligned}
	\right.
	\end{equation*}
	Then $\widetilde\eta(t,u)=\eta(t,u)$ as long as $t\ge 0$ and $\widetilde\eta(t,u)\in \mathcal{J}^{\beta+\varepsilon}_{\beta-\varepsilon}\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta/2)$. Using  \eqref{e-entrancetime1} we can define the entrance time map $e\colon\mathcal{J}^{\beta+\varepsilon}\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\to [0,\infty[$ as
	\[
	e(u):=\inf\Set{t\in [0,\infty[\,|  \mathcal{J}\bigl(\widetilde\eta(t,u)\bigr)\leq \beta -\varepsilon}.
	\]
	Arguing as before we can prove that $e$ is continuous; moreover, $e$ is clearly even. Take any $A\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $i^*(A)\geq k$ and $\mathcal{J}(u)\leq \beta+\varepsilon$ for $u\in A$. Let $T:=\max_{u\in A} e(u)<\infty$ ($A$ is compact). Set $h:=\widetilde\eta(T,\cdot)$ and note that $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and
	\[
	h\bigl(A\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\bigr) \subset \mathcal{J}^{\beta-\varepsilon}.
	\]
	Therefore
	\[
	i^*\bigl(A\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\bigr)\leq 
	i^*\Bigl(h\bigl(A\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\bigr)\Bigr)\leq  k-1
	\]
	and
	\begin{equation}\label{e-LSvaluse}
	k\leq i^*(A)\leq \gamma \bigl(\overline B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\cap A\bigr)+
	i^*\bigl(A\setminus B(\mathcal{K}^\beta,\delta)\bigr)
	\leq \gamma(\mathcal{K}^\beta)+k-1.
	\end{equation}
	Thus $\mathcal{K}^\beta\neq \emptyset$ and, since $\gamma(\mathcal{K}^\beta)\le1$, we conclude $\gamma(\mathcal{K}^\beta)=1$.	If $\beta_k=\beta_{k+1}$ for some
	$k\geq 1$, then \eqref{e-LSvaluse} implies $\gamma(\mathcal{K}^{\beta_k})\geq 2$, a contradiction. Hence we get an infinite sequence
	$\beta_1<\beta_2<\cdots$
	of critical values which contradicts our assumption that $\mathcal{K}$ consists of a finite number of distinct orbits.

	If $(\bar v,\bar w)\in \mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$ then
	$$J(t\bar  v,t\bar w+\psi)-J'(\bar v,\bar w)\left(\frac{t^2-1}{2}\bar v,\frac{t^2-1}{2}\bar w+t\psi\right)\leq J(\bar v,\bar w)$$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(\bar v,\bar w)\in\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$, $\psi\in\mathcal{W}$, $t\geq 0$. We define
	$$D(t,\psi):=J(t \bar v,t\bar w+\psi)-J(\bar v,\bar w)-J'(\bar v,\bar w)\left(\frac{t^2-1}{2}\bar v,\frac{t^2-1}{2}\bar w+t\psi\right)$$
	and observe that
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		D(t,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f(x,\bar v+\bar w)\cdot\left(\frac{t^2-1}{2}(\bar v+\bar w)+t\psi\right)\\
		+F(x,\bar v+\bar w)-F\bigl(x,t(\bar v+\bar w)+\psi\bigr)\,dx.
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	For fixed $x,v,w\in\mathbb{R}^3$, define the map $\phi\colon[0,\infty[\,\times\,\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ as follows:
	\[
	\phi(t,\psi):=
	f(x,v+w)\cdot\left(\frac{t^2-1}{2}(v+w)+t\psi\right)+F(x,v+w)-F\bigl(x,t(v+w)+\psi\bigr).
	\]
	We prove that $\phi(t,\psi)\leq 0$ for all $t\geq 0$ and all $\psi\in\mathbb{R}^3$. This is clear if $v+w=0$, thus let $v+w\ne 0$ and define $\zeta := t(v+w)+\psi$.                                                                                                    
	From (F4) we have
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\phi(t,\psi) \le \, & f(x,v+w)\cdot\left(\frac{t^2-1}{2}(v+w)+t\bigl(\zeta-t(v+w)\bigr)\right)\\
		& +\frac12 f(x,v+w)\cdot(v+w)-F(x,\zeta) \\
		= \, & -\frac12t^2 f(x,v+w)\cdot(v+w) + t f(x,v+w)\cdot\zeta - A|\zeta|^2\\
		& + A|\zeta|^2-F(x,\zeta).
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	If $A>0$ is large enough, then the quadratic form (in $t$ and $\zeta$) above is negative definite. Moreover, $A|\zeta|^2-F(x,\zeta)$ is bounded from above owing to the superquadraticity of $F$ implied by (F3) and (N3). Hence $\phi(t,\psi)\to -\infty$ as $t+|\psi|\to\infty$ and $\phi$ attains its maximum at some $(t,\psi)$ with $t\geq 0$.  If $t=0$, then $\phi(t,\psi)=\phi(0,\psi)\leq 0$. If $t>0$, then
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
	\partial_t\phi(t,\psi) & = f(x,v+w)\cdot\bigl(t(v+w)+\psi\bigr) - f\bigl(x,t(v+w)+\psi\bigr)\cdot(v+w) = 0, \\
	\nabla_\psi\phi(t,\psi) & = tf(x,v+w) - f(x,t(v+w)+\psi) = 0.
	\end{split}\end{equation*} 
	Using the latter equation in the former, we see that both terms in the former are positive (because $f(x,v+w)\cdot(v+w)>0$ from (F3 and (F4)) and $f(x,v+w)\cdot\psi=0$. This and (F5) imply
	\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
	\phi(t,\psi) & = \frac{t^2-1}{2}f(x,v+w)\cdot(v+w)+F(x,v+w)-F\bigl(x,t(v+w)+\psi\bigr)\\
	& \le 0.\qedhere
	\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
head: environment

label: L:BrezLieb
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:BrezLieb}
	Let $\mathbf{U}_n\in L^{\Phi}$ bounded such that
	$\mathbf{U}_n\to \mathbf{U}$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
	Then
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n)-F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U})\, dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})\, dx.
	\]
head: environment

label: e-*
title: Proof
body_md:
Note that
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n)-F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U})\, dx
		&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\, dtdx\\
		&=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}\, dxdt
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	and $f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})$ is bounded
	in $L^{\Psi}$ owing to (F3) and Lemmas \ref{L:all} \textit{(iv)} and \ref{L:forC1}.
	Thus for every $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$
	\begin{eqnarray}\label{e-*}
	\int_{\Omega}|f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}|\,dx
	\leq |f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})|_{\Psi}
	|\mathbf{U}\chi_{\Omega}|_{\Phi}.
	\end{eqnarray}
	From \cite[Definition III.IV.2, Corollary III.IV.5 and Theorem III.IV.14]{RaoRen}, the space $L^\Phi$ has an absolutely continuous norm (cf. \cite[Definition III.I.13]{RaoRen}), so \eqref{e-*} yields that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$
	such that, if $|\Omega|<\delta$, then
	\[
	\int_{\Omega}|f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}|\,dx<\varepsilon
	\]
	for every $n$, i.e., $f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}$ is uniformly integrable.
	Using \eqref{e-*} once more we see that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with 
	$|\Omega|<\infty$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-tight}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\Omega}f(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}\,dx<\varepsilon.
	\end{equation}
	As a matter of fact, since $\Phi\circ|\mathbf{U}|\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$, there exists a sequence $\Omega_n\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ such that each $\Omega_n$ has finite measure and
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi(|\mathbf{U}|\chi_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\Omega_n})\,dx = \lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi(|\mathbf{U}|)\chi_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\Omega_n}\,dx = 0,
	\]
	where in the first equality we used that $\Phi(t)=0\Leftrightarrow t=0$. In view of (N1) and Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iii)}, this yelds $\lim_n|\mathbf{U}\chi_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\Omega_n}|_\Phi=0$. If we take $\Omega = \Omega_{\bar{n}}$ for some sufficiently large $\bar{n}$ such that $|\mathbf{U}\chi_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\Omega}|_{\Phi} < \varepsilon(\sup_k|f(\cdot,\mathbf{U}_k-\mathbf{U}+t\mathbf{U})|_{\Psi})^{-1}$, then \eqref{e-tight} holds.
	                                                                             
	Since $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ a.e. on $\mathbb{R}^3$, it follows from Vitali's convergence theorem that
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n)-F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U})\,dx & \to
	\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,t\mathbf{U})\cdot\mathbf{U}\,dxdt\\
	& =\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})\,dx.\qedhere
	\end{aligned}\]
head: environment

label: L:WeakStrong
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:WeakStrong}
	If $\mathbf{U}_n\rightharpoonup\mathbf{U}$ in $L^{\Phi}$ and
	$\mathfrak{I}(\mathbf{U}_n)\to \mathfrak{I}(\mathbf{U})$,
	then $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ in $L^{\Phi}$.
head: environment

label: e-i3
title: Proof
body_md:
We show that $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$ up to a subsequence.
	Since $\mathfrak{I}(\mathbf{U}_n)\to \mathfrak{I}(\mathbf{U})$, we have
	\begin{equation} \label{e-i3}
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})\,dx.
	\end{equation}
	Then from (F2) we infer that for every $0<r\leq R$
	\begin{equation} \label{e-mrR}
	m_{r,R}:=\inf_{\substack{x,u_1,u_2\in\mathbb{R}^3\\ r\leq|u_1-u_2|\\|u_1|,|u_2|\leq R} }	\frac{1}{2}\bigl(F(x,u_1)+F(x,u_2)\bigr)-F\left(x,\frac{u_1+u_2}{2}\right)>0.
	\end{equation} 
	Observe that from \eqref{e-i3}  and (F2) there holds
	$$
	0
	\leq \limsup_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac12\bigl(F(x,\mathbf{U}_n) + F(x,\mathbf{U})\bigr)
	- F\left(x,\frac{\mathbf{U}_n+\mathbf{U}}{2}\right)\,dx
	\leq 0.
	$$
	Therefore, setting
	$$
	\Omega_n:=\Set{x\in\mathbb{R}^3|\left|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}\right|\geq r \text{ and } |\mathbf{U}_n|,|\mathbf{U}|\leq R},
	$$
	from \eqref{e-mrR} we have
	$$
	|\Omega_n| m_{r,R}
	\leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac12\bigl(F(x,\mathbf{U}_n) + F(x,\mathbf{U})\bigr)
	- F\left(x,\frac{\mathbf{U}_n+\mathbf{U}}{2}\right)\, dx,
	$$
	thus $|\Omega_n|\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$. Since $0<r\leq R$ are arbitrarily chosen, we deduce
	$$
	\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}\hbox{ a.e. in }\mathbb{R}^3.
	$$
	In view of Lemma \ref{L:BrezLieb}, we obtain
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n)\, dx-\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U})\, dx\to\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U})\, dx
	\]
	and hence
	$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U})\, dx\to0.$$
	From (F3) and Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iii)}, we get $|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|_\Phi\to 0$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P:DefOfm(u)} Conditions  (I1)--(I8) are satisfied and
	there is a Cerami sequence $(v_n,w_n)\in\mathcal{M}$ at level $c_{\mathcal{N}}$,

label: e-I7check
title: Proof
body_md:
Setting $X:=\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$,
	$X^+:=\mathcal{V}\times\{0\}$, and $X^-:=\{0\}\times\mathcal{V}$ we check the assumptions (I1)--(I8) for the functional $J\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ 
	given by
	\[
	J(v,w)=\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^2_\mathcal{D}-I(v,w)
	\]
	(cf. \eqref{e-J} and \eqref{e-DefOfXi}). Recall that $\|(v,w)\|^2=\|v\|_{\mathcal{D}}^2+|w|_{\Phi}^2$. The convexity and differentiability of $I$, (F3), and Lemma \ref{L:WeakStrong} yield the following.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I1)] $I|_{\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}}\in \mathcal{C}^1(\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W},\mathbb{R})$ and $I(v,w)\geq I(0,0)=0$ for every $(v,w)\in \mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$.
		\item[(I2)] If $v_n\to v$ in $\mathcal{V}$ and $w_n\rightharpoonup w$ in $\mathcal{W}$, then $\displaystyle\liminf_nI(v_n,w_n)\geq I(v,w)$.
		\item[(I3)] If $v_n\to v$ in $\mathcal{V}$, $w_n\rightharpoonup w$ in $\mathcal{W}$, and $I(v_n,w_n)\to I(v,w)$, then $(v_n,w_n)\to (u,w)$.
	\end{itemize}

	Moreover,
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I6)] There exists $r>0$ such that $\inf_{\|v\|_\mathcal{D}=r}J(v,0)>0$.
	\end{itemize}
	As a matter of fact, from (F3) and (N2) there exist $C>0$ (cf. the proof of Lemma \ref{L:emb}) such that for any $v\in\mathcal{V}$
	$$J(v,0)=\|v\|_\mathcal{D}^2 -\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,v)\,dx
	\geq\|v\|_\mathcal{D}^2-C\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|v|^6\,dx
	\geq\|v\|_\mathcal{D}^2-C\|v\|_\mathcal{D}^6,$$
	thus (I6) is satisfied taking $r$ sufficiently small. Note that
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I4)] $\|v\|_\mathcal{D}+I(v,w)\to\infty$ as $\|(v,w)\|\to\infty$.
	\end{itemize}
	To see this, let $\|(v_n,w_n)\|\to\infty$. If $\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}\to\infty$, then we are done; otherwise, up to a subsequence $\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}$ is bounded and, a fortiori, so is $|v_n|_\Phi$. This yields $|v_n+w_n|_\Phi\ge|w_n|_\Phi-|v_n|_\Phi\to\infty$. Using (F3) and Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iv)} we have
	\[
	I(v_n,w_n)\ge c_2\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi(|v_n+w_n|)\,dx\to\infty.
	\]
	
	This, together with the uniform strict convexity of $F$, implies
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I5)] If $(v,w)\in\mathcal{M}$, then $I(v,w)<I(v,w+\psi)$ for every $\psi\in \mathcal{W}\setminus\{0\}$.
	\end{itemize}

	Next, we prove 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I7)] $I\bigl(t_n(v_n,w_n)\bigr)/t_n^2\to\infty$ if $t_n\to\infty$ and $v_n\to v$ for some $v\neq 0$.
	\end{itemize}
	Observe that from (F3)
	\begin{equation} \label{e-I7check}
	\begin{split}
	\frac{I\bigl(t_n(v_n,w_n)\bigr)}{t_n^2}&=
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{F\bigl(x,t_n(v_n+w_n)\bigr)}{t_n^2}\,dx\\
	&\geq c_2
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\Phi(t_n|v_n+w_n|)}{t_n^2}\,dx\\ 
	&= c_2
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\Phi(t_n|v_n+w_n|)}{t_n^2|v_n+w_n|^2}|v_n+w_n|^2\,dx.
	\end{split}
	\end{equation} 
	Take $R_0>0$ such that $v\neq 0$ in $L^2(B_{R_0})$.
	In view of (N3), there exists $C>0$ such that
	$$C\Phi(t)\geq t^2\quad\hbox{for }t\geq 1.$$
	Then, writing
	\[
	B_R=\bigl(B_R\cap\{|v_n+w_n|\ge1\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(B_R\cap\{|v_n+w_n|<1\}\bigr),
	\]
	we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e-estim}
	\int_{B_R}|v_n+w_n|^2\,dx\le C\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\Phi(t_n|v_n+w_n|)}{t_n^2}\,dx+|B_R|
	\end{equation}
	and $I\bigl(t_n(v_n,w_n)\bigr)/t_n^2\to\infty$ (up to a subsequence) if $v_n+w_n$ is unbounded in $L^2(B_R,\mathbb{R}^3)$ for some $R\geq R_0$. Now, suppose that $v_n+w_n$ is bounded in $L^2(B_R,\mathbb{R}^3)$ for every $R\geq R_0$. We can assume passing to a subsequence that $v_n\to v$ a.e. and $w_n\rightharpoonup w$ in $L^2_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ for some $w$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, let 
	\begin{equation}\label{e-aetoinfI7}
	\Omega_n := \Set{x\in\mathbb{R}^3|\left|v_n(x)+w_n(x)\right|\ge\varepsilon}.
	\end{equation}
	We claim that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\limsup_n|\Omega_n|>0$. Arguing by contradiction, suppose $|\Omega_n|\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$. Then $v_n+w_n\to 0$ in measure, so up to a subsequence $v_n+w_n\to 0$ a.e., hence $w_n\to -v$ a.e. and  $w_n\rightharpoonup -v$ in $L^2_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$. Since $\nabla\times w_n=0$ in the distributional sense, the same is true of $v$, thus there exists $\xi\in H^1_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ such that $v=\nabla \xi$ due to \cite[Lemma 1.1 (i)]{Leinfelder}. As $\nabla\cdot(\nabla \xi)=\nabla\cdot v =0$, it follows that $\xi$ is harmonic and so is $v$. Recalling that $v\in\mathcal{D}$, we obtain $v=0$ as in the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Hel}. This is a contradiction.
	Taking $\varepsilon$ in \eqref{e-aetoinfI7} such that $\limsup_n|\Omega_n|>0$, we obtain
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\Phi(t_n|v_n+w_n|)}{t_n^2|v_n+w_n|^2}|v_n+w_n|^2\,dx \ge \int_{\Omega_n}\frac{\Phi(t_n|v_n+w_n|)}{t_n^2|v_n+w_n|^2}|v_n+w_n|^2\,dx \to \infty.
	\]
	
	Finally, Proposition \ref{P:uv_N} shows that
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(I8)']
		$\displaystyle\frac{t^2-1}{2}I'(v,w)(v,w)+tI'(v,w)(0,\psi)+I(v,w)-I(tv,tw+\psi)\leq 0$
		for every $t\geq 0$, $v\in\mathcal{V}$, and $w,\psi\in\mathcal{W}$,
	\end{itemize}
	which is a stronger version of (I8).
	
	Applying Theorem \ref{T:Link1} we conclude.

label: L:DefofW
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: e-mI
title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(a)} Let $v\in L^{\Phi}$. 
	Since  $w\in\mathcal{W}\mapsto I(v,w)\in\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, strictly convex, and coercive,  there exists a unique $w(v)\in\mathcal{W}$ such that (\ref{e-DefofW(u)}) holds.
	We show that the map $w\colon L^{\Phi}\to\mathcal{W}$ is continuous. Let $v_n\to v$ in $L^{\Phi}$. Since 
	\begin{equation}\label{e-mI}
	0\leq I\bigl(v_n,w(v_n)\bigr)\leq I(v_n,0),
	\end{equation}
	$w(v_n)$ is bounded and we may assume  $w(v_n)\rightharpoonup w_0$ for some $w_0\in\mathcal{W}$.
	Observe that by the (sequential) lower semicontinuity of $I$ we get
	\[\begin{split}
	I\bigl(v,w(v)\bigr) & \le I(v,w_0)\leq \liminf_nI\bigl(v_n,w(v_n)\bigr)\leq\limsup_n I\bigl(v_n,w(v_n)\bigr)\\
	& \leq \lim_nI\bigl(v_n,w(v)\bigr)=I\bigl(v,w(v)\bigr),
	\end{split}\]
	hence $w(v)=w_0$ from the uniqueness of $w(v)$, and from Lemma \ref{L:WeakStrong} we have $v_n+w(v_n)\to v+w(v)$ in $L^{\Phi}$, which yields $w(v_n)\to w(v)$ in $\mathcal{W}$.
	
	\textit{(b)} This follows from (\ref{e-mI}), (F3), and Lemma \ref{L:all} \textit{(iv)}.

label: L:Coercive
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Coercive} If $\beta>0$ and
	$v_n\in\mathcal{V}$ are such that $J\bigl( m(v_n)\bigr)\leq\beta$ and $\lim_n(1+\|v_n\|)(J\circ m)'(v_n)=0$, then $v_n$ is bounded.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us write $m(v_n)=(v_n,w_n)\in\mathcal{M}$ and suppose by contradiction $\lim_n\|(v_n,w_n)\|=\infty$. Since $w_n=w(v_n)$, $\|(v_n,w_n)\|\to\infty$ if and only if $\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}\to\infty$.
	Let $\bar{v}_n:=v_n/\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}$ and $\bar{w}_n:=w_n/\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}$.
	Assume 
	\[
	\lim_n\sup_{y\in\mathbb{Z}^3}\int_{B(y,R)}|\bar{v}_n|^2\,dx=0
	\]
	for some fixed $R>\sqrt{3}$. From Lemma \ref{L:Conv}, $\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi(|\bar{v}_n|)\,dx=0$ and  we obtain a contradiction: recalling that $J'(v_n,w_n)(0,w_n)=0$,
	Proposition \ref{P:uv_N} with $t_n=s/\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}$ and $\psi_n=-t_nw_n$ implies that for every $s>0$
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\beta & \ge\limsup_nJ(v_n,w_n) \\
		& \ge \limsup_nJ(s\bar{v}_n,0)-\lim_nJ'(v_n,w_n)\left(\frac{t_n^2-1}{2}v_n,-\frac{t_n^2+1}{2}w_n\right)\\
		& =\limsup_nJ(s\bar{v}_n,0)\overset{\text{(F3)}}{\ge}\frac{s^2}{2}-\lim_nc_1\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Phi(s|\bar v_n|)\,dx
		=\frac{s^2}{2},
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	which is impossible. Hence $\liminf_n\int_{B(y_n,R)}|\bar{v}_n|^2\,dx>0$, where $y_n\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ maximizes $y\in\mathbb{Z}^3\mapsto\int_{B(y,R)}|\bar{v}_n|^2\,dx\in\mathbb{R}$. Since $\mathcal{M}$ and $J$ are invariant with respect to $\mathbb{Z}^3$-translations, we may assume that
	$$\int_{B_R}|\bar{v}_n|^2\,dx\geq c>0$$
	for some constant $c$ and every $n\gg1$. This implies that, up to a subsequence, $\bar{v}_n\rightharpoonup\bar v\ne 0$ in $\mathcal{D}$, $\bar{v}_n\to\bar{v}$ in $L^2_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $\bar{v}_n\to\bar v$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$ for some $\bar v\in\mathcal{D}$.	From (F4),
	\[\begin{split}
	2J(v_n,w_n) & - J'(v_n,w_n)(v_n,w_n) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(x,v_n+w_n)\cdot(v_n+w_n)\,dx\\
	& - 2\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}F(x,v_n+w_n)\,dx \ge 0,
	\end{split}\]
	so $J(v_n,w_n)$ is bounded from below and, using (F3),
	$$\alpha \le \frac{J(v_n,w_n)}{\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}^2}\le \frac{1}{2}\|\bar{v}_n\|_\mathcal{D}^2-c_2\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\Phi(|v_n+w_n|)}{|v_n+w_n|^2}|\bar{v}_n+\bar{w}_n|^2\,dx$$
	for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Hence it suffices to show that the integral on the right-hand side above tends to $\infty$. We can argue as in the proof of (I7) in Proposition \ref{P:DefOfm(u)}. In particular, \eqref{e-estim} holds with $\bar v_n+\bar w_n$ instead of $v_n+w_n$ and $\|v_n\|_\mathcal{D}$ instead of $t_n$ and, if $\Omega_n$ is as in \eqref{e-aetoinfI7} (again, with $v_n+w_n$ replaced with $\bar v_n+\bar w_n$), then $\lim_n|\Omega_n|>0$ along a subsequence.

label: C:Ceramibdd
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C:Ceramibdd}
	Let $\beta>0$. There exists $M_\beta>0$ such that for every $v_n\in\mathcal{V}$ satisfying $0\le\liminf_nJ\bigl(m(v_n)\bigr)\le\limsup_nJ\bigl(m(v_n)\bigr)\le\beta$ and $\lim_n(1+\|v_n\|)J'\bigl(m(v_n)\bigr)=0$ there holds $\limsup_n\|v_n\|\le M_\beta$.

title: Proof
body_md: If no finite bound $M_\beta$ exists, for every $k$ there exists a sequence $v_n^k\in X$ satisfying the assumptions above and such that $\limsup_n\|v_n^k\|\ge k$. In particular, there exists $n(k)$ such that $-1/k<J\bigl(m(v_{n(k)}^k)\bigr)<\beta+1/k$, which yields $0\le\liminf_kJ\bigl(m(v_{n(k)}^k)\bigr)\le\limsup_kJ\bigl(m(v_{n(k)}^k)\bigr)\le\beta$. In the same way we prove $\lim_k\bigl(1+\|v_{n(k)}^k\|\bigr)(J\circ m)'\bigl(v_{n(k)}^k\bigr)=0$ and $\limsup_k\|v_{n(k)}^k\|=\infty$, a contradiction with Lemma \ref{L:Coercive}.

body_md: \label{L:CoEmb} If $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is a Lipschitz domain with finite measure, then $H^1(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in $L^\Phi(\Omega)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $u_n\rightharpoonup 0$ in $H^1(\Omega)$. Then $u_n\rightharpoonup 0$ in $L^6(\Omega)$ and $u_n\to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, up to a subsequence, a.e. in $\Omega$. From (N2), for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $C_\varepsilon$ such that $\Phi(t)\le \varepsilon t^6$ for $t>C_\varepsilon$, whence
	\[\begin{split}
	\int_{\Omega} \Phi(|u_n|)\,dx & = \int_{\Omega\cap\{|u_n|\le C_\varepsilon\}} \Phi(|u_n|)\,dx + \int_{\Omega\cap\{|u_n| > C_\varepsilon\}} \Phi(|u_n|)\,dx\\
	& \le \int_{\Omega\cap\{|u_n|\le C_\varepsilon\}} \Phi(|u_n|)\,dx +\varepsilon\sup_k|u_k|_6^6.
	\end{split}\]
	From the dominated convergence theorem and since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we have $\int_{\Omega} \Phi(|u_n|)\,dx\to 0$ and, due to Lemma \ref{L:all} (iii), $|u_n|_\Phi\to 0$.

	If $v_n\rightharpoonup v$ in $\mathcal{D}$, then $w(v_n)\rightharpoonup w(v)$ in $\mathcal{W}$ and, after passing to a subsequence, $w(v_n)\to w(v)$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

label: e-1
title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from the definition \eqref{e-DefofW(u)} of $w(v)$ that
	\begin{equation} \label{e-1}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f\bigl(x,v_n+w(v_n)\bigr)\cdot z\,dx = 0 = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f\bigl(x,v+w(v)\bigr)\cdot z\,dx \quad \forall z \in \mathcal{W}.
	\end{equation}
	Since $v_n$ is bounded, so is $w(v_n)$ from Lemma \ref{L:DefofW} \textit{(b)}, hence we can assume $w(v_n)\rightharpoonup w_0$ for some $w_0$. In addition, since $v_n\to v$ in $L^2_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$, $v_n\to v$ a.e. after passing to a subsequence.
	
	Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be bounded and let $\zeta\in \mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)$, $0\le\zeta\le1$, such that $\zeta=1$ in $\Omega$. From (F3) and Lemmas \ref{L:all} \textit{(ii)}, \ref{L:forC1}, and \ref{L:CoEmb}, there exist $C>0$ such that
	\begin{equation} \label{e-10}
	\begin{split}0 & \le\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\left|f\bigl(x,v_n+w(v_n)\bigr)\right|\left|v_n-v\right|\zeta\,dx\\
	& \le C\left|\Phi'\bigl(|v_n+w(v_n)|\bigr)\right|_{\Psi} |(v_n-v)\zeta|_\Phi\to 0.
	\end{split}\end{equation}
	Choose $R>0$ such that $\textup{supp}\zeta\subset B_R$. In view of (N3), $w(v_n)$ is bounded in $L^2(B_R,\mathbb{R}^3)$. As a matter of fact, $w(v_n)\chi_{\{|w(v_n)|<1\}}$ is of course bounded in $L^2(B_R,\mathbb{R}^3)$, while
	\[
	\int_{B_R\cap\{|w(v_n)|\ge 1\}}|w(v_n)|^2\,dx \le C \int_{B_R\cap\{|w(v_n)|\ge 1\}}\Phi(|w(v_n)|)\,dx \le C
	\]
	for some $C>0$. From \cite[Lemma 1.1 \textit{(i)}]{Leinfelder}, there exists $\xi_n\in H^1(B_R)$ such that $w(v_n)=\nabla\xi_n$. We can assume $\int_{B_R}\xi_n\,dx = 0$, so that from the Poincar\'e inequality
	\[
	\|\xi_n\|_{H^1(B_R)}\le C|\nabla\xi_n|_{L^2(B_R)}\le C
	\]
	for some $C>0$. Hence in view of Lemma \ref{L:CoEmb}, up to a subsequence, $\xi_n\to \xi$ in  $L^\Phi(B_R)$  for some $\xi\in H^1(B_R)$. Similarly as in \eqref{e-10}, we have
	\begin{equation} \label{e-11}
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\left|f\bigl(x,v_n+w(v_n)\bigr)\right|\left|\nabla\zeta\right|\left|\xi_n-\xi\right|\,dx=0.
	\end{equation}
	The limits in \eqref{e-10} and \eqref{e-11} are 0 also if $f\bigl(x,v_n+w(v_n)\bigr)$ is replaced with $f(x,v+\nabla\xi)$. Combining \eqref{e-1}--\eqref{e-11} we obtain
	\begin{equation} \label{e-2}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Bigl(f\bigl(x,v_n+w(v_n)\bigr)-f(x,v+\nabla\xi)\Bigr)\cdot\bigl(v_n-v+w(v_n)-\nabla\xi\bigr)\zeta\,dx\to0,
	\end{equation}
	where we have taken $z = \nabla\bigl((\xi_n-\xi)\zeta\bigr)$ in \eqref{e-1}. We prove that  $v_n+w(v_n) \to v+ \nabla\xi$ a.e. in $\Omega$. The convexity of $F$ implies that 
	\[
	F\left(x,\frac{\mathbf{U}_1+\mathbf{U}_2}{2}\right)\geq F(x,\mathbf{U}_1)+f(x,\mathbf{U}_1)\cdot\frac{\mathbf{U}_2-\mathbf{U}_1}{2}
	\]
	and
	\[
	F\left(x,\frac{\mathbf{U}_1+\mathbf{U}_2}{2}\right)\geq F(x,\mathbf{U}_2)+f(x,\mathbf{U}_2)\cdot\frac{\mathbf{U}_1-\mathbf{U}_2}{2}.
	\]
	Summing these inequalities and using (F2), we obtain that for every $0<r\leq R$ and every $|\mathbf{U}_1-\mathbf{U}_2|\ge r$, $|\mathbf{U}_1|,|\mathbf{U}_2| \le R$
	\[\begin{split}
	m_{r,R} & \le \frac12\bigl(F(x,\mathbf{U}_1)+F(x,\mathbf{U}_2)\bigr) - F\left(x,\frac{\mathbf{U}_1+\mathbf{U}_2}2\right)\\
	& \le \frac14\bigl(f(x,\mathbf{U}_1)-f(x,\mathbf{U}_2)\bigr)\cdot(\mathbf{U}_1-\mathbf{U}_2)
	\end{split}\]
	where $m_{r,R}$ is defined in \eqref{e-mrR}. Since $\zeta=1$ in $\Omega$, it follows from \eqref{e-2} that $v_n+w(v_n) \to v+ \nabla\xi$ a.e. in $\Omega$ as claimed. Since $w(v_n)\rightharpoonup w_0$, we have $w_0=\nabla\xi$ and by the usual diagonal procedure we obtain a.e. convergence to $v+w_0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. 
	Take any $w\in\mathcal{W}$ and observe that by Vitali's convergence theorem 
	$$0=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\langle f(x,v_n+w(v_n)), w\rangle\,dx\to \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\langle f(x,v+w_0), w\rangle\,dx.$$
	The uniqueness of $w(v)$ (see Lemma \ref{L:DefofW}) implies that $w_0=w(v)$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C:Jweaklycont}
	If $(v_n,w_n)\in\mathcal{M}$ and $(v_n,w_n)\rightharpoonup (v_0,w_0)$ in $\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$, then  $J'(v_n,w_n)\rightharpoonup J'(v_0,w_0)$, i.e.,

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From Lemma \ref{L:DefofW} \textit{(a)} we get $w_n=w(v_n)$. In view of Proposition \ref{P:ae}, we may assume  $v_n+w_n\to v_0+w_0$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (where $w_0=w(v_0)$).
	For $(\phi,\psi)\in\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{W}$ we have
	\[\begin{split}
	J'(v_n,w_n)(\phi,\psi) & -J'(v_0,w_0)(\phi,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}(\nabla v_n-\nabla v_0)\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx\\
	& -\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\bigl(f(x,v_n+w_n)-f(x,u_0+w_0)\bigr)\cdot(\phi+\psi)\,dx. 
	\end{split}\]
                                                                                                                                         
                 
                                                            
                                                                               
               
                    
	Arguing as in the proof of Lemma \ref{L:BrezLieb}, we prove that
	\[
	\bigl(f(x,v_n+w_n)-f(x,u_0+w_0)\bigr)\cdot(\phi+\psi)
	\]
	is uniformly integrable and tight, hence from Vitali's convergence theorem
	\[
	J'(v_n,w_n)(\phi,\psi)\to J'(v_0,w_0)(\phi,\psi).\qedhere
	\]

More precisely, if $|v_n|_\Phi\to 0$, then \eqref{e-convergence} with $u_n=0$ holds by the same argument. This is impossible because $J\bigl(m(v_n)\bigr)\to c_\mathcal{N}>0$. Hence \eqref{e-boundedaway} with $u_n=0$ is satisfied and we can assume, up to translating by $y_n$, that $\int_{B_R}|v_n|^2\,dx\ge\varepsilon$, whence $v\ne 0$.

	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}

		&\geq J(v,w)-\frac12J'(v,w)(v,w) =\mathcal{J}(v,w).
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	Since $(v,w)\in\mathcal{N}$, $J(v,w)=c_{\mathcal{N}}$ and $\mathbf{U}=v+w$ solves \eqref{e-Curl} due to Proposition \ref{P:var}.
	
	Note that here we have \emph{not} assumed $\mathcal{K}$ has finitely many distinct orbits.

label: L:Oapprox
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Oapprox}
	If $\mathbf{U}\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$, then there exists $\mathbf{U}_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$ such that $\lim_n|\nabla\mathbf{U}_n-\nabla \mathbf{U}|_{2}=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$, there exists $\mathbf{V}_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$ such that $\lim_n|\nabla \mathbf{V}_n-\nabla\mathbf{U}|_{2}=0$. Let $$\mathbf{U}_n(x):=\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}g^{-1}\mathbf{V}_n(gx)\,d\mu(g)=\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}g^T\mathbf{V}_n(gx)\,d\mu(g),$$ where $\mu$ is the Haar measure of $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$ (note that $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$ is compact).
	
	For every $e\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$ we have
	\[
	\mathbf{U}_n(ex)=\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}g^T\mathbf{V}_n(gex)\,d\mu(g)=e\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}g'^T\mathbf{V}_n(g'x)\,d\mu(g')=e\mathbf{U}_n(x),
	\]
	i.e., $\mathbf{U}_n\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$. Moreover, $\mathbf{U}_n\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$ because so does $\mathbf{V}_n$.
	
	First we prove that $|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|_{2^*}\to 0$. From Jensen's inequality there holds
	\[\begin{split}
	|\mathbf{U}_n-\mathbf{U}|_{2^*}^{2^*} & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left|\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}g^T\mathbf{V}_n(gx)-\mathbf{U}(x)\,d\mu(g)\right|^{2^*}dx\\
	& \leq\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left|g^T\mathbf{V}_n(gx)-\mathbf{U}(x)\right|^{2^*}dx\,d\mu(g)\\ & =\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left|g^T\mathbf{V}_n(gx)-g^T\mathbf{U}(gx)\right|^{2^*}dx\,d\mu(g)\\
	& =\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left|\mathbf{V}_n(gx)-\mathbf{U}(gx)\right|^{2^*}dx\,d\mu(g)\\ &
	=\int_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}|\mathbf{V}_n-\mathbf{U}|_{2^*}^{2^*}\,d\mu(g)=|\mathbf{V}_n-\mathbf{U}|_{2^*}^{2^*}\to 0.
	\end{split}\]
	Finally, $\mathbf{U}_n$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$ because, similarly as before,
	\[
	|\nabla \mathbf{U}_n-\nabla \mathbf{U}_m|_2\le|\nabla \mathbf{V}_n-\nabla\mathbf{V}_m|_2\to 0,
	\]
	hence $\mathbf{U}_n\to\mathbf{U}$ in $\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N.\mathbb{R}^N)$.

body_md:
\label{P:Density}
There holds
\[
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}=\overline{\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N_*,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{H}\cap\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}},

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inclusion `$\supset$' is obvious since $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$ is closed. Now let $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$. Since $\mathbf{U}\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$, in view of Lemma \ref{L:Oapprox} there exists $\mathbf{U}^n\in\mathcal{C}^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$ such that $\mathbf{U}^n=(\mathbf{U}_1^n,\dots,\mathbf{U}_N^n)\to\mathbf{U}$ in $\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$.

For every $n$, let $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n,\mathbf{U}_\tau^n,\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\in\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$ defined in Lemma \ref{L:dec} and associated with $\mathbf{U}^n$, i.e.
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)$ is the projection of $\mathbf{U}^n(x)$ onto $\textup{span}\{(x_1,x_2,0)\}$,
	\item $\mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)$ is the projection of $\mathbf{U}^n(x)$ onto $\textup{span}\{(-x_2,x_1,0)\}$,
	\item $\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n(x)$ is the projection of $\mathbf{U}^n(x)$ onto $\textup{span}\{e_i\}$.
\end{itemize}
In particular, $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n,\mathbf{U}_\tau^n,\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N_*,\mathbb{R}^N)$, they vanish outside a sufficiently large ball in $\mathbb{R}^N$ (in fact, $\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$) and $\mathbf{U}_n(x)=\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)+\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N_*$. Moreover, $\nabla\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)$, $\nabla\mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)$, $\nabla\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n(x)$ are pairwise orthogonal in $\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{N^2}$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N_*$.

This implies that $\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\to\mathbf{U}$ in $\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$, hence we are only left to prove that $\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{H}$.

Since $\mathbf{U}^n\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$, for every $g\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$ and every $z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-2}$
\[
\widetilde{g}\mathbf{U}^n(0,0,z)=\mathbf{U}^n\bigl(\widetilde{g}(0,0,z)\bigr)=\mathbf{U}^n(0,0,z),
\]
which yields $\mathbf{U}_1^n(0,0,z)=\mathbf{U}_2^n(0,0,z)=0$ (just take $g=-I_2$). Moreover,
\[
\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)=\frac{\mathbf{U}_n\cdot(x_1,x_2,0)}{|(x_1,x_2)|^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\, \text{ and } \, \mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)=\frac{\mathbf{U}_n\cdot(-x_2,x_1,0)}{|(x_1,x_2)|^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-x_2\\
x_1\\
0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
therefore, from the uniform continuity of $\mathbf{U}^n$,
\[
\lim_{y\to0}\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)=\lim_{y\to0}\mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)=0
\]
uniformly with respect to $z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-2}$. Hence we can extend $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n$ and $\mathbf{U}_\tau^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^N$ by setting them equal to $0$ on $\{0\}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{N-2}$ and obtain that $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n,\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $\mathbf{U}^n(x)=\mathbf{U}_\rho^n(x)+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n(x)+\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.

To prove that $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\in\mathcal{H}$, first we notice that $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n=\mathbf{U}^n-\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and, using Taylor's expansion,
\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
	\left(\mathbf{U}^n-\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\right)(x) = \, & \left(\mathbf{U}^n-\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\right)(0,z)\\
	& +\left[\nabla\left(\mathbf{U}^n-\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\right)(0,z)\right]
	\begin{pmatrix}
	y & 0
	\end{pmatrix}
	+o(y)\\
	= \, & \left[\nabla\left(\mathbf{U}^n-\sum_{i=3}^N\mathbf{U}_{\zeta,i}^n\right)(0,z)\right]
	\begin{pmatrix}
	y & 0
	\end{pmatrix}
	+o(y)
\end{split}\end{equation*} 
as $y\to 0$, thus $\mathbf{U}_\rho^n+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\in\mathcal{H}$. Finally, note that $|\mathbf{U}_\tau^n|\le|\mathbf{U}_\rho^n+\mathbf{U}_\tau^n|$, whence $\mathbf{U}_\tau^n\in\mathcal{H}$.

If, moreover, $f$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem \ref{T:ScalVec} and $h(x,\alpha w)=f(x,\alpha)w$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and $w=|(\xi_1,\xi_2)|^{-1}(-\xi_2,\xi_1,0)$, $\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2>0$, then $J(u)=E(\mathbf{U})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$. We show that the pointwise gradient a.e. of $\mathbf{U}=(\mathbf{U}_1,\mathbf{U}_2,0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ is also the distributional gradient of $\mathbf{U}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$. As a matter of fact, for $\partial_1\mathbf{U}_1$ we have
\[\begin{split}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u(x)\frac{-x_2}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}\partial_1\varphi(x)\,dx\\
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left(\partial_1u(x)\frac{x_2}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}-u(x)\frac{x_1x_2}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\right)\varphi(x)\,dx\\
=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\partial_1\left(u(x)\frac{-x_2}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}\right)\varphi(x)\,dx<\infty
\end{split}\]
for every $\varphi\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)$ because $\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u(x)\frac{x_1x_2}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\varphi(x)\,dx<\infty$ for $u\in X$.	
For $\partial_1\mathbf{U}_2$ similarly we get
\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u(x)\frac{x_1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}\partial_1\varphi(x)\,dx\\
	=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left(\partial_1u(x)\frac{x_1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}+u(x)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}-\frac{x_1^2}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\right)\right)\varphi(x)\,dx\\
	=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\partial_1\left(u(x)\frac{x_1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}\right)\varphi(x)\,dx<\infty
\end{split}\end{equation*}
for every $\varphi\in\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
The remaining cases are similar. 

Now observe that $\mathbf{U}\in L^{2^*}(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{F}$. Moreover,
\[
\partial_1\mathbf{U}_1=\partial_1u\frac{x_2}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}-u\frac{x_1x_2}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)
\]
and
\[
\partial_1\mathbf{U}_2=-\partial_1u\frac{x_1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}-u\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}-\frac{x_1^2}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\right)\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)
\]
because $u\in X$.
Again, the remaining cases are similar and we infer $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{F}$.

Now suppose that $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$ and, due to Proposition \ref{P:Density}, let $\mathbf{B}_n\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N_*,\mathbb{R}^N)\cap\mathcal{H}\cap\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$ such that $\lim_n|\nabla\mathbf{B}_n-\nabla\mathbf{U}|_2=0$ and let $b_n\colon\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$-invariant such that $\mathbf{B}_n$ and $b_n$ satisfy \eqref{e-uU}.

We prove that $b_n\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$. Of course $b_n\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N_*)$ and, since $|\mathbf{B}_n|=|b_n|$, $b_n\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^N)\subset L^{2^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $b_n(x)=O(y)$ uniformly with respect to $z$ as $y\to0$, therefore
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{b_n^2}{r^2}\,dx<\infty.
\]
Moreover, $\nabla\mathbf{B}_n\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^{N\times N})$, where
\[
\nabla\mathbf{B}_n(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
-x_2\\
x_1\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\nabla b_n(x)^T+\frac{b_n(x)}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1x_2 & -x_1^2 & 0\\
x_2^2 & -x_1x_2 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
and the second summand above is square-integrable because
\[\begin{split}
\left|\frac{1}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1x_2 & -x_1^2 & 0\\
x_2^2 & -x_1x_2 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\right|_{\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}}\\
=\frac{1}{(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{3/2}}\Bigg|
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
x_2 & -x_1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\Bigg|_{\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}},
\end{split}\]
where $|\cdot|_{\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}}$ stands for the matrix norm in $\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$. It follows that $\nabla b_n\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$, thus $b_n\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$.

Since $\lim_n|b_n-u|_{2^*}=\lim_n|\mathbf{B}_n-\mathbf{U}|_{2^*}=0$, it is enough to prove that $b_n$ is a Cauchy sequence in $X$, therefore we compute
\[\begin{split}
\|b_n-b_m\|^2 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla(b_n-b_m)\cdot\nabla(b_n-b_m)+\frac{(b_n-b_m)(b_n-b_m)}{r^2}\,dx\\
& =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla(\mathbf{B}_n-\mathbf{B}_m)\cdot\nabla(\mathbf{B}_n-\mathbf{B}_m)\,dx=|\nabla(\mathbf{B}_n-\mathbf{B}_m)|_2^2\to0
\end{split}\]
as $n,m\to\infty$.

Next, since $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$, as in the first part we have that the pointwise divergence a.e. of $\mathbf{U}$ is also the distributional divergence of $\mathbf{U}$, hence $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{U}=0$ follows from explicit computations

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  

Finally, observe that if $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ and $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$ satisfy \eqref{e-uU}, then $\|u\|^2=|\nabla\mathbf{U}|_2^2=|\nabla\times\mathbf{U}|_2^2$ and $F\bigl(x,u(x)\bigr)=H\bigl(x,\mathbf{U}(x)\bigr)$ for a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first part follows directly from Lemma \ref{L:DivFree}. As in \cite[Proposition 1]{AzzBenDApFor}, we have that $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}=\Set{\mathbf{U}\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})|\mathcal{S}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{U}}$ and that $E(\mathcal{S}\mathbf{U})=E(\mathbf{U})$ for every $\mathbf{U}\in\textup{Fix}(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O})$, where $\mathcal{S}$ is defined in \eqref{e-S}.
	
	Finally, if $\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}$ and $v\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ satisfy \eqref{e-uU}, then arguing as in Lemma \ref{L:DivFree} there holds
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla\times\mathbf{U}\cdot\nabla\times\mathbf{V}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla\mathbf{U}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{V}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\frac{uv}{r^2}\,dx
	\]
	and
	\[\begin{split}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}h\bigl(x,\mathbf{U}(x)\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{V}(x)\,dx & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}h\biggl(x,\frac{u}{r}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\biggr)\cdot\frac{v(x)}{r}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\,dx\\
	& =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f\left(x,u(x)\right)\frac{1}{r}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\cdot\frac{v(x)}{r}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\,dx\\
	& =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f\bigl(x,u(x)\bigr)v(x)\,dx,
	\end{split}\]
	thus the conclusion follows from Theorem \ref{T:Palais}.

label: L:pqDec
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:pqDec}
	Let $1\le p\le 2^*\le q<\infty$. If $u\in L^{2^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, then
	\[
	|u\chi_{\{|u|\le 1\}}|_q^q,\;|u\chi_{\{|u|>1\}}|_p^p\le|u|_{2^*}^{2^*}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There holds
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^q\chi_{\{|u|\le 1\}}\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^{2^*}\chi_{\{|u|\le1\}}\,dx\le|u|_{2^*}^{2^*}
	\]
	and
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^p\chi_{\{|u|>1\}}\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^{2^*}\chi_{\{|u|>1\}}\,dx\le|u|_{2^*}^{2^*}.\qedhere
	\]
head: environment

label: L:Lions2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Lions2}
	Suppose that $u_n,v_n\in\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ are bounded and $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$-invariant and that $u_n$ satisfies \eqref{e-LionsCond} for every $R>0$. Then
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|f(x,v_n)u_n|\,dx=0.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $1<p<2^*<q<\infty$, define $\Phi(t):=\int_0^{|t|}\min\{s^{p-1},s^{q-1}\}\,ds$, and note that $\Phi$ satisfies \eqref{e-LionsPhi}. (F2) implies that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $C_\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ we have $|f(x,t)|\le\varepsilon|t|^{2^*-1}+C_\varepsilon|\Phi'(t)|$. Moreover
	\[\begin{split}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\Phi'(v_n)u_n|\,dx & = \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\Phi'(v_n)u_n|\chi_{\{|u_n|>1\}}\,dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\Phi'(v_n)u_n|\chi_{\{|u_n|\le 1\}}\,dx\\
	& =:A_n+B_n.
	\end{split}\]
	Concerning the first integral $A_n$, Lemmas \ref{L:Lions} and \ref{L:pqDec} imply that, for some $C>0$,
	\[\begin{split}
	A_n&= \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n|^{p-1}\chi_{\{|v_n|>1\}}|u_n|\chi_{\{|u_n|>1\}}\,dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n|^{q-1}\chi_{\{|v_n|\le 1\}}|u_n|\chi_{\{|u_n|>1\}}\,dx\\
	& \le\left(|v_n\chi_{\{|v_n|>1\}}|_p^{p-1}+\big||v_n|^{q-1}\chi_{\{|v_n|\le 1\}}\big|_{{(p-1)/p}}\right)|u_n\chi_{\{|u_n|>1\}}|_p\\
	& \le C\left(|v_n\chi_{\{|v_n|>1\}}|_p^{p-1}+|v_n\chi_{\{|v_n|\le 1\}}|_q^{q(p-1)/p}\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\Phi(u_n)\,dx\right)^\frac{1}{p}\\
	& \le C\sup_k\|v_k\|^\frac{2^*(p-1)}{p}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\Phi(u_n)\,dx\right)^\frac{1}{p}\to0
	\end{split}\]
	because $\bigl(|v_n|^{q-1}\bigr)^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\chi_{\{|v_n|\le 1\}}\le|v_n|^q\chi_{\{|v_n|\le 1\}}$.
	
	Similar computations hold for the second integral $B_n$, therefore we have
	\[
	\limsup_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|f(x,v_n)u_n|\,dx\le\varepsilon\sup_k|v_k|_{2^*}^{2^*-1}\sup_k|u_k|_{2^*}^{2^*}
	\]
	and conclude letting $\varepsilon\to0^+$.
head: environment

label: L:I678
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:I678}
	(a) There exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for every $0<\delta<\delta_0$
	\[
	\inf\Set{J(u)|u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}} \text{ and } \|u\|=\delta}>0
	\]
	(b) Suppose $f$ satisfies (F3). If $t_n\to\infty$ and $u_n\to u_0\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}\setminus\{0\}$, then
	\[
	\lim_n\frac{1}{t_n^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,t_nu_n)\,dx=\infty.
	\]
	(c) Suppose $f$ satisfies (F4). For every $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ and every $t\ge0$ $$\frac{t^2-1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,u)u\,dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,u)\,dx-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,tu)\,dx\le0.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(a)} From (F2) and the embeddings $X\hookrightarrow\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)\hookrightarrow L^{2^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, there exists $C>0$ such that for every $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,u)\,dx\le C|u|_{2^*}^{2^*}\le C\|u\|^{2^*},
	\]
	whence
	\[
	J(u)\ge\frac12\|u\|^2-C\|u\|^{2^*}
	\]
	and the statement holds true for $\delta_0\ll1$.
	
	\textit{(b)} Since $X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ is locally compactly embedded into $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$, up to a subsequence $u_n\to u_0$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Moreover, there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\limsup_n|\Omega_n|>0$, where $\Omega_n:=\Set{x\in\mathbb{R}^N|\lVert u_n(x)\rVert\ge\varepsilon}$, for otherwise $u_n\to0$ in measure and consequently, up to a subsequence, a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$. From (F3)
	\[
	\frac{1}{t_n^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,t_nu_n)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(x,t_nu_n)}{t_n^2|u_n|^2}|u_n|^2\,dx\ge\varepsilon^2\int_{\Omega_n}\frac{F(x,t_nu_n)}{t_n^2|u_n|^2}\,dx\to\infty
	\]
	as $n\to\infty$.
	
	\textit{(c)} For fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and $u\in\mathbb{R}$ we prove that $\phi(t)\le0$ for every $t\ge0$, where $$\phi(t):=\frac{t^2-1}{2}f(x,u)u+F(x,u)-F(x,tu).$$ This is trivial for $u=0$, so suppose $u\ne0$.
	Note that $\phi(1)=0$, so it is enough to prove that $\phi$ is nondecreasing on $[0,1]$ and nonincreasing on $[1,\infty[$. This is the case in view of (F4) and because
	\[
	\phi'(t)=tf(x,u)u-f(x,tu)u=t|u|u\biggl(\frac{f(x,u)}{|u|}-\frac{f(x,tu)}{|tu|}\biggr)
	\]
	for $t>0$, therefore $\phi(t)\le0$ for every $t\ge0$ as $\phi\in\mathcal{C}^1([0,\infty[)$.

label: L:Mbeta
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(a)} Let $u_n\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ as in the assumptions. Suppose that $u_n$ is unbounded and define $\bar{u}_n:=u_n/\|u_n\|$. Passing to a subsequence we can assume that $\lim_n\|u_n\|=\infty$. Similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Lions2}, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $C_\varepsilon>0$ such that
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,\bar{u}_n)\,dx\leq\varepsilon|\bar{u}_n|_{2^*}^{2^*}+ C_\varepsilon\Phi(\bar{u}_n),
	\]
	where $\Phi$ is defined therein. If $\bar{u}_n$ satisfies \eqref{e-LionsCond} for every $R>0$ (hence the same holds for $s\bar{u}_n$, $s\ge0$), then in view of Lemma \ref{L:Lions}
	\[
	\limsup_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,s\bar{u}_n)\,dx\leq \varepsilon s^2\limsup_n|\bar{u}_n|_{2^*}^{2^*}
	\]
	for every $\varepsilon>0$, hence $\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,s\bar{u}_n)\,dx=0$.
	Then applying Lemma \ref{L:I678} \textit{(c)} with $u=u_n$ and $t=s/\|u_n\| =: t_n$ we obtain, up to a subsequence, that for every $s\ge0$
	\[\begin{split}
	\beta&\ge\limsup_nJ(u_n)\ge\limsup_nJ(s\bar{u}_n)-\lim_n\frac{t_n^2-1}{2}J'(u_n)u_n\\
	&=\limsup_nJ(s\bar{u}_n)\ge\frac{s^2}{2}-\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,s\bar{u}_n)\,dx=\frac{s^2}{2},
	\end{split}\]
	a contradiction. Hence $\lim_n\int_{B((0,z_n),R)}|\bar{u}_n|^2\,dx>0$ up to a subsequence for some $R>\sqrt{N-K}$ and $z_n\subset\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$, where $z_n$ maximizes $z\mapsto\int_{B((0,z),R)}|u_n|^2\,dx$. Exploiting the $\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$-invariance, we can assume that
	\[
	\int_{B_R}|\bar{u}_n|^2\,dx\ge c
	\]
	for $n\gg1$ and some $c>0$.
	
	There follows that there exists $\bar{u}\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}\setminus\{0\}$ such that, up to a subsequence, $\bar{u}_n\rightharpoonup\bar{u}$ in $X$ and $\bar{u}_n\to\bar{u}$ in $L^2_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
	
	From (F4), $2J(u_n)-J'(u_n)u_n=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,u_n)u_n-2F(x,u_n)\,dx\ge0$, thus $J(u_n)$ is bounded and due to (F3) we obtain
	\[
	o(1)=\frac{J(u_n)}{\|u_n\|^2}\le \frac12-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(x,u_n)}{|u_n|^2}|\bar{u}_n|^2\,dx\to-\infty,
	\]
	which is a contradiction.	
	This shows that $u_n$ is indeed bounded. If by contradiction there exists no upper bound $M_\beta$, then for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $u_n^k\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ as in the statement such that $\limsup_n\|u_n^k\|>k$. Then, as in Corollary \ref{C:Ceramibdd}, it is easy to build a subsequence $u_{n(k)}^k\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ that is unbounded, again a contradiction.
	
	\textit{(b)} Assume that there are finitely many critical orbits of $J$. From (G) we easily see that $$\kappa:=\inf\big\{\|u-v\|:u\ne v\text{ and }J'(u)=J'(v)=0\big\}>0.$$
	
	Let $u_n,v_n$ be as in the statement. In view of \textit{(a)}, they are bounded. If $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,u_n)(u_n-v_n)\,dx$ or $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,v_n)(u_n-v_n)\,dx$ do not converge to $0$, then in view of Lemma \ref{L:Lions2} and the $\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$-invariance there exist $R>\sqrt{N-K}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $$\int_{B_R}|u_n-v_n|^2\,dx\ge\varepsilon.$$
	We can assume that $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ and $v_n\rightharpoonup v$ in $X$, so $u\ne v$. Hence $J'(u)=J'(v)=0$ and consequently $$\liminf_n\|u_n-v_n\|\ge\|u-v\|\ge\kappa,$$ in contrast with the assumptions.
	
	Therefore it follows that
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,u_n)(u_n-v_n)\,dx=\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,v_n)(u_n-v_n)\,dx=0
	\]
	and, finally,
	\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
	\|u_n-v_n\|^2= J'(u_n)(u_n-v_n)-J'(v_n)(u_n-v_n)\\
	+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\bigl(f(x,u_n)-f(x,v_n)\bigr)(u_n-v_n)\,dx\to0.\qedhere
	\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $\mathcal{N}$ contains all the nontrivial critical points of $J$. Applying Theorem \ref{T:Link1} we obtain a Cerami sequence $u_n\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ at the level $c:=\inf_\mathcal{N} J>0$. Lemma \ref{L:Mbeta}\textit{(a)} implies that there exists $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ such that $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ up to a subsequence, thus $J'(u)=0$.
	
	If by contradiction $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x,u_n)u_n\,dx\to0$, then similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Mbeta} \textit{(b)} we infer that $u_n\to0$, in contrast with $J(u_n)\to c$. Hence, again similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Mbeta} \textit{(b)}, $u\ne0$.
	
	Fatou's Lemma and (F4) imply
	\[\begin{split}
	c & = \lim_nJ(u_n) = \lim_n\left(J(u_n) - \frac12J'(u_n)u_n\right)\\
	& = \lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12 f(x,u_n)u_n - F(x,u_n)\,dx \ge\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12 f(x,u)u-F(x,u)\,dx\\
	& = J(u) - \frac12J'(u)u = J(u) \ge c.
	\end{split}\]
	
	Now assume $f$ is odd in $u$, which implies that $J$ is even. The existence of infinitely many geometrically distinct critical points of $J$ follows directly from Theorem \ref{T:CrticMulti} \textit{(b)}. As for the fact that the ground state solution is nonnegative, since $J(v)=J(|v|)$ and $J'(v)v=J'(|v|)|v|$ for every $v\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$, we obtain that $|u|$ is again a ground state solution.
