label: L:positive
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:positive}
	Suppose that $f$ does not depend on $y$ and satisfies (F5). Then there exists $w\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ such that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(z,w)\,dx>\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla_z w|^2\,dx$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $R\ge3$ we define a continuous function $\phi_R\colon\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\phi_R(t)=0$ for $|t|<1$ and for $|t|>R+1$, $\phi_R(t)=1$ for $2\leq |t|\leq R$ and $\phi_R$ is affine for $1\le|t|\le2$ and for $R\le|t|\le R+1$. Then let $w_R(x):=u_0\phi_R(|y|)\phi_R(|z|)$. Observe that $w_R\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ and there exist constants $C_1,C_2>0$ such that
	\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} F(z,w_R)\,dx\geq \, & C_1R^N\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-K}}F(z,u_0)\\
		& -C_2R^{N-1}\sup_{R\leq |u|\leq R+1}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-K}}F(z,u)\\
		& -C_2\sup_{1\leq |u|\leq 2}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-K}}F(z,u)
	\end{split}\end{equation*}
	and
	$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla_z w|^2\leq C_2R^{N-1}.$$
	Then the statement holds true for $R\gg1$.
head: environment

label: e-bddaway
title: Proof
body_md:
First we prove that $J$ has the mountain pass geometry. Let $w\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ as in Lemma \ref{L:positive}. From
	Lemma \ref{L:I678} \textit{(a)},
	there exists $0<\delta<\|w\|$ such that $\inf\Set{J(u)|u\in X_{\mathcal{O}} \text{ and } \|u\|=\delta}>0$.
	Moreover, for every $\lambda>0$ we have
	\[\begin{split}
	J\bigl(w(\lambda\cdot,\cdot)\bigr)= \, & \frac{1}{2\lambda^{K-2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla_y w|^2+\frac{a}{r^2}|w|^2\,dx\\
	& +\frac{1}{\lambda^K}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1}{2}|\nabla_z w|^2-F(z,w)\,dx\to-\infty
	\end{split}\]
	as $\lambda\to 0^+$. Consequently, the existence of a Palais--Smale sequence $u_n\in X$ for $J|_{X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}}$ at the mountain pass level $c>0$ follows. Such a sequence is bounded because (F5) holds: for every $n\gg1$
	\[\begin{split}
	c+1 & +\|u_n\|\ge J(u_n)-\frac1\gamma J'(u_n)(u_n)\\
	& =\left(\frac12-\frac1\gamma\right)\|u_n\|^2+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac1\gamma f(u_n)u_n-F(u_n)\,dx\ge\left(\frac12-\frac1\gamma\right)\|u_n\|^2.
	\end{split}\]
	
	Now, suppose by contradiction that \eqref{e-LionsCond} holds for every $R>0$. Fix $R>\sqrt{N-K}$ such that \eqref{e-LionsCond} holds with the supremum being taken over $\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$. Since $F$ and $(z,u)\mapsto f(z,u)u$ satisfy \eqref{e-LionsPhi} uniformly with respect to $z\in\mathbb{R}^{N-K}$, from Lemma \ref{L:Lions} and arguing as in Lemma \ref{L:Lions2} we obtain
	\[
	c=\lim_nJ(u_n)-\frac12J'(u_n)u_n=\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12 f(z,u_n)u_n-F(z,u_n)\,dx=0,
	\]
	which is a contradiction. Then there exist $R>\sqrt{N-K}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that, up to a subsequence,
	\begin{equation}\label{e-bddaway}
	\int_{B((0,z_n),R)}u_n^2\,dx\ge\varepsilon
	\end{equation}
	where $z_n\in\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$ maximizes $z\mapsto\int_{B((0,z),R)}|u_n|^2\,dx$.
	Since $J$ is invariant with respect to $\mathbb{Z}^{N-K}$ translations, up to replacing $u_n$ with $u_n(\cdot-z_n)$ we can suppose that $z_n=0$. Since $u_n$ is bounded, there exists $u\in X_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ such that $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ in $X$, which in turn implies that $J'(u)=0$ and that $u_n\to u$ in $L^2\bigl(B_R\bigr)$ and a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$; in particular, $u\ne 0$ because \eqref{e-bddaway} holds.

\label{L:equisym}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g_1\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$ and define $g:=(g_1,I_2)\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)\times\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$. Note that
	$$g\pi^{-1}(x)=\pi^{-1}(\widetilde{g_1}x)$$
	for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$, therefore
	\[
	\widetilde{g_1}\mathbf{U}(x)=\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)}\mathbf{U}\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)=\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi(\widetilde{g_1}x)}\mathbf{U}(\widetilde{g_1}x)=\mathbf{U}	(\widetilde{g_1}x).\qedhere
	\]

label: L:compact
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$ define $\mathbf{V}(\xi):=\frac{\mathbf{U}(\pi(\xi))}{\psi(\pi(\xi))}$ for $\xi\in\mathbb{S}^3\setminus\{Q\}$. Note that $\mathbf{V}\in H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and, similarly as in \cite[Lemma 3.1]{ClPis}, $|\nabla \mathbf{U}|_2=\|\mathbf{V}\|_{H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)}$ and $|\mathbf{U}|_{6}=\|\mathbf{V}\|_{L^6(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)}$,
	where 
	$$\|\mathbf{V}\|^2_{H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)}=\int_{\mathbb{S}^3}|\nabla_\mathfrak{g}\mathbf{V}|^2+\frac34|\mathbf{V}|^2\,dV_\mathfrak{g}$$ is the norm in 
	$H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $\nabla_\mathfrak{g}$ is the gradient on $\mathbb{S}^3$ \cite{Aubin,ONeill}.
	Therefore $\mathbf{U}\mapsto\mathbf{V}$ is an isometric isomorphism between $\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and between $L^6(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $L^6(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$. Note that, since $\mathbf{U}$ is $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)$-symmetric, then $\mathbf{V}(g\xi)=\widetilde{g_1}\mathbf{V}(\xi)$ for every $g=(g_1,g_2)\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)\times\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$ and, consequently, $|\mathbf{V}|$ is $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)\times\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$-invariant, or equivalently $\mathcal{O}(2)\times\mathcal{O}(2)$-invariant. 
	
	Let $\mathbf{U}_n\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$ such that $\mathbf{U}_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$. Then $\mathbf{V}_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $H^1(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and, up to a subsequence, $\mathbf{V}\to0$ a.e. in $\mathbb{S}^3$; this implies that $|\mathbf{V}_n|\rightharpoonup0$ in $H^1(\mathbb{S}^3)$ and so, in view of \cite[Lemma 5]{Ding}, $|\mathbf{V}_n|\to0$ in $L^6(\mathbb{S}^3)$. Hence $\mathbf{V}_n\to0$ in $L^6(\mathbb{S}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$ and so $\mathbf{U}_n\to0$ in $L^6(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$.

label: L:decom
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:decom}
	If $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$, then $\mathbf{U}_\rho,\mathbf{U}_\tau,\mathbf{U}_\zeta\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$.
head: environment

label: e-tau
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove that $\mathbf{U}_\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$. Let $\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}$, $g_i=
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	\cos\alpha_i & -\sin\alpha_i\\
	\sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$, $i\in\{1,2\}$, and set $g=
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	g_1 & 0\\
	0 & g_2
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	$. We want to prove that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-tau}
	\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)}\mathbf{U}_\tau\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)=\widetilde{g_1}\mathbf{U}_\tau(x)
	\end{equation}
	provided
	\[
	\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)}\mathbf{U}\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)=\widetilde{g_1}\mathbf{U}(x).
	\]
	
	We compute the two sides of \eqref{e-tau} separately. We use the convention that $\mathbb{R}^3=\mathbb{R}^{3\times1}$ and treat the scalar product in $\mathbb{R}^3$ as matrix multiplication.
	
	As for the right-hand side we have
	\[\begin{split}
	\widetilde{g_1}\mathbf{U}_\tau(x) & =\frac{\widetilde{g_1}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	}{x_1^2+x_2^2}=\frac{
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\cos\alpha_1-x_1\sin\alpha_1\\
	-x_2\sin\alpha_1+x_1\cos\alpha_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\\
	x_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	}{x_1^2+x_2^2}\\
	& =\frac{-x_2\mathbf{U}_1(x)+x_1\mathbf{U}_2(x)}{x_1^2+x_2^2}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\cos\alpha_1-x_1\sin\alpha_1\\
	-x_2\sin\alpha_1+x_1\cos\alpha_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right).
	\end{split}\]
	
	Let us write $\pi=
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	\pi_1\\
	\pi_2\\
	\pi_3
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	$. As for the left-hand side we have
	\[\begin{split}
	\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)}\mathbf{U}_\tau\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)\\
	=\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)}\frac{
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\mathbf{U}^T\Bigl(\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)\Bigr)
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	}{\pi_1^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)+\pi_2^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)}\\
	=\frac{
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)\widetilde{g_1}^T
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	}{\pi_1^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)+\pi_2^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)}.
	\end{split}\]
	
	Let us compute
	\[
	g\pi^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{|x|^2+1}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	2x_1\cos\alpha_1-2x_2\sin\alpha_1\\
	2x_1\sin\alpha_1+2x_2\cos\alpha_1\\
	2x_3\cos\alpha_2-(|x|^2-1)\sin\alpha_2\\
	2x_3\sin\alpha_2+(|x|^2-1)\cos\alpha_2
	\end{smallmatrix}\right),
	\]
	\[
	\pi\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)=\frac{1}{|x|^2+1-2x_3\sin\alpha_2\mp(|x|^2-1)\cos\alpha_2}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	2x_1\cos\alpha_1-2x_2\sin\alpha_1\\
	2x_1\sin\alpha_1+2x_2\cos\alpha_1\\
	2x_3\cos\alpha_2-(|x|^2-1)\sin\alpha_2
	\end{smallmatrix}\right),
	\]
	\[
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)\widetilde{g_1}^T=
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	\mathbf{U}_1(x)\cos\alpha_1-\mathbf{U}_2(x)\sin\alpha_1\\
	\mathbf{U}_1(x)\sin\alpha_1+\mathbf{U}_2(x)\cos\alpha_1\\
	\mathbf{U}_3(x)
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)^T,
	\]
	\[
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)\widetilde{g_1}^T
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))
	\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	=\frac{2\bigl(-x_2\mathbf{U}_1(x)+x_1\mathbf{U}_2(x)\bigr)}{|x|^2+1-2x_3\sin\alpha_2-(|x|^2-1)\cos\alpha_2},
	\]
	and
	\[
	\pi_1^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)+\pi_2^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)=\frac{4x_1^2+4x_2^2}{\bigl(|x|^2+1-2x_3\sin\alpha_2-(|x|^2+1)\cos\alpha_2\bigr)^2},
	\]
	so for the left-hand side we have
	\[\begin{split}
	\frac{
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\mathbf{U}^T(x)\widetilde{g_1}^T
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-\pi_2(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	\pi_1(g\pi^{-1}(x))\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	}{\pi_1^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)+\pi_2^2\bigl(g\pi^{-1}(x)\bigr)}\\
	=\frac{-x_2\mathbf{U}_1(x)+x_1\mathbf{U}_2(x)}{x_1^2+x_2^2}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	-x_2\cos\alpha_1-x_1\sin\alpha_1\\
	-x_2\sin\alpha_1+x_1\cos\alpha_1\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	\end{split}\]
	and \eqref{e-tau} holds.
	
	Similar computations hold for $\mathbf{U}_\rho$, so $\mathbf{U}_\rho\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$. Finally, $\mathbf{U}_\zeta=\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}_\rho-\mathbf{U}_\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$.

label: L:inf
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:inf}
	$\mathcal{Y}$ is infinite dimensional.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e=
	\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}
	0 & -1\\
	1 & 0
	\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)
	\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2)$ and let $\mathcal{X}$, resp. $\mathcal{Z}$, be the subspace of $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$ consisting in the vector fields $\mathbf{U}$ such that
	\[
	\mathbf{U}(x)=\frac{u(x)}{r}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	x_1\\
	x_2\\
	0
	\end{pmatrix}
	, \text{ resp. }\mathbf{U}(x)=u(x)
	\begin{pmatrix}
	0\\
	0\\
	1
	\end{pmatrix},
	\]
	for some $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$-invariant $u\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$. In order to prove that $\mathcal{Y}$ is infinite dimensional, we build an isomorphism between $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ and an isomorphism between $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$. The conclusion will follow from the fact that $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}$ is infinite dimensional and that, in view of Lemmas \ref{L:dec} and \ref{L:decom}, we get the decomposition $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)}=\mathcal{X}\oplus\mathcal{Y}\oplus\mathcal{Z}$.
	
	For every $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{X}$ define $\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}(x):=\mathbf{U}(\widetilde{e}x)$. It is clear that $\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}\in\mathcal{Y}$ and that $\mathbf{U}\mapsto\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}$ is an isomorphism.
	
	Now consider $\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{X}$ and let $u\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}$-invariant such that $\mathbf{U}(x)=\frac{u(x)}{r}
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	x_1\\
	x_2\\
	0
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	$. Define $\overline{\mathbf{U}}(x):=u(x)
	\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
	0\\
	0\\
	1
	\end{smallmatrix}\right)
	$. By similar arguments to those used in the proof of Lemma \ref{L:DivFree} it is easy to check that $\overline{\mathbf{U}}\in\mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3)$. Finally, explicit computations show that $\overline{\mathbf{U}}$ is $\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}(2\times2)$-symmetric (hence $\overline{\mathbf{U}}\in\mathcal{Z}$) and trivially $\mathbf{U}\mapsto\overline{\mathbf{U}}$ is an isomorphism.

then there exist $(\lambda_j)_{j=1}^m\in[0,\infty[^m$ and $(\sigma_k)_{k=1}^n\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that

\]

Although there are no explicit restrictions on $K$ in Theorem \ref{T:main2}, the example in \eqref{e-exK} shows that we could need $K$ not to be too large. As a matter of fact, since $r_j>1$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, there holds

label: P:ex
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P:ex}
	Let $K\ge2$ and $\nu_j\ge0$, $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, and define
	\[
	F(u)=\sum_{j=1}^K\nu_j|u_j|^{2_\#}.
	\]
	Then $\displaystyle\limsup_{|u|\to\infty}\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}=\max_{j=1,\dots,K}\nu_j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By taking $u_j=0$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ but one we easily obtain $\displaystyle\limsup_{|u|\to\infty}\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}\ge\max_{j=1,\dots,K}\nu_j$. Since $\displaystyle F(u)\le\max_{j=1,\dots,K}\nu_j\sum_{j=1}^K|u_j|^{2_\#}$, it suffices to prove that for every $u\in\mathbb{R}^K$
	\[
	\left(|u_1|^{2_\#}+\dots+|u_K|^{2_\#}\right)^{1/{2_\#}}\le\left(u_1^2+\dots+u_K^2\right)^{1/2}.
	\]
	To this aim, we will prove that the function $\varphi\colon]0,\infty[\to]0,\infty[$ is decreasing, where $\varphi(t):=(b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t)^{1/t}$ for some $b_1,\dots,b_K>0$. From
	\[
	\varphi'(t)=\varphi(t)\left(\frac{b_1^t\ln b_1+\dots+b_K^t\ln b_K}{t(b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t)}-\frac1{t^2}\ln(b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t)\right)
	\]
	we have that $\varphi'(t)<0$ is equivalent to
	\[
	b_1^t\ln(b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t)+\dots+b_K^t\ln(b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t)>b_1^t\ln b_1^t+\dots+b_K^t\ln b_K^t,
	\]
	which is true because $\ln$ is increasing.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $r_1,r_2>1$ such that $r_1+r_2=2_\#$ and define
	\[
	F(u)=|u_1|^{r_1}|u_2|^{r_2}.
	\]
	Then $\displaystyle\limsup_{|u|\to\infty}\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}=\sqrt{r_1^{r_1}r_2^{r_2}/2_\#^{2_\#}}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Observe that, for $u_2\ne0$, $\displaystyle\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}=\varphi\left(\frac{|u_1|}{|u_2|}\right)$, with $\displaystyle\varphi(t):=\frac{t^{r_1}}{(t^2+1)^{2_\#}}$. Since $\displaystyle\max\varphi=\varphi\left(\!\sqrt{\frac{r_1}{r_2}}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{r_1^{r_1}r_2^{r_2}}{2_\#^{2_\#}}}$, there holds
	\[
	\sqrt{\frac{r_1^{r_1}r_2^{r_2}}{2_\#^{2_\#}}}\ge\limsup_{|u|\to\infty}\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}\ge\limsup_{\substack{u_1=\sqrt{r_1/r_2}u_2\\ |u_2|\to\infty}}\frac{F(u)}{|u|^{2_\#}}=\sqrt{\frac{r_1^{r_1}r_2^{r_2}}{2_\#^{2_\#}}}.\qedhere
	\]

label: L:cbb
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:cbb}
	If (F0)--(F2) and \eqref{e-etas} hold, then $J|_{\mathcal{D}}$ is coercive and bounded from below.

title: Proof
body_md:
From (F1) and (F2), for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $c_\varepsilon>0$ such that $F(u)\le c_\varepsilon u^2+(\varepsilon+\eta_\infty)|u|^{2_\#}$ for every $u\in\mathbb{R}$. In view of Theorem \ref{T:GN}, for every $u\in\mathcal{D}$ we have
	\[\begin{split}
		J(u)&\ge\frac12|\nabla u|_2^2-c_\varepsilon |u|_2^2-(\varepsilon+\eta_\infty)|u|_{2_\#}^{2_\#}\\
		&\ge\frac12|\nabla u|_2^2-c_\varepsilon \rho^2-(\varepsilon+\eta_\infty)\rho^{4/N}C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\nabla u|_2^2\\
		&=\left(\frac12-(\varepsilon+\eta_\infty)\rho^{4/N}C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}\right)|\nabla u|_2^2-c_\varepsilon\rho^2,
	\end{split}\]
	hence the statement holds true for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$.

label: e-ineqeta0
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $u\in\mathfrak{D}\setminus\{0\}$ and note that
	\[
	J(s\star u)=s^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla u|^2-\frac{F(s^{N/2}u)}{(s^{N/2})^{2_\#}}\,dx.
	\]
	If $\eta_0=\infty$, then $\displaystyle\lim_{s\to0^+}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(s^{N/2}u)}{(s^{N/2})^{2_\#}}\,dx=\infty$. If $\eta_0<\infty$, then
	\[
	\limsup_{s\to0^+}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla u|^2-\frac{F(s^{N/2}u)}{(s^{N/2})^{2_\#}}\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla u|^2-\eta_0|u|^{2_\#}\,dx,
	\]
	hence the statement holds true if $u\in\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{e-ineqeta0}
		\frac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2\,dx<\eta_0\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^{2_\#}\,dx.
	\end{equation}
	Let $w\in\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}$ be the unique positive radial solution to $-\Delta v+\frac2Nv=v^{2_\#-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ \cite{Kwong}. Then (cf. \cite{Weinstein}) $w$ is such that $$|w|_2^{4/N}=\frac{2_\#}{2C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}}$$ and equality holds in the Gagliardo--Nirenberg interpolation inequality (Theorem \ref{T:GN}). If we define $u(x):=w(tx)$ for some $t>0$, then $u\in\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}$ and \eqref{e-ineqeta0} become, respectively,
	\begin{equation}\label{e-ineqs}
		|w|_2^2\le\rho^2t^N \quad \text{and} \quad t^2|\nabla w|_2^2<2\eta_0|w|_{2_\#}^{2_\#}.
	\end{equation}

Let $u_n\in\mathfrak{D}$ such that $\lim_nJ(u_n)=\inf_{\mathfrak{D}}J$. In view of Lemma \ref{L:cbb} there exists $u\in\mathfrak{D}$ such that, up to a subsequence, $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $u_n\to u$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$ as $n\to\infty$.

	\textit{(b)} Since $F$ is even, choosing $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}$ we can replace $u_n$ with its Schwarz rearrangement $u_n^*$ and we obtain another minimizing sequence for $J|_{\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}}$ with the additional property that each $u_n^*$ is radially nonincreasing. label: L:Schwarz
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Schwarz}
	Let $L$ be a positive integer and, for every $\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}$, let $k(\ell)\ge2$ be an integer as well. Define $\bar{k}:=\max_{\ell=1,\dots,L}k(\ell)$. For every $\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}$ and every $j\in\{1,\dots,k(\ell)\}$ let $\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}\colon[0,\infty[\to[0,\infty[$ satisfy (at least) one of the following:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}$ is increasing;
		\item $\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}$ is nondecreasing, continuous, and $\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}(0)=0$.
	\end{itemize}
	Finally, define $\widetilde{F}\colon\mathbb{R}^{\bar{k}}\to\mathbb{R}$ as
	\[
	\widetilde{F}(u)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L\prod_{j=1}^{k(\ell)}\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}(|u_{i_j}|), \quad 1\le i_1<\dots<i_{k(\ell)}\le\bar{k}.
	\]
	                                                                                                                                                                                     
	Then for every measurable $u\colon\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^{\bar{k}}$ that vanishes at infinity there holds
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widetilde{F}(u)\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widetilde{F}(u^*)\,dx,
	\]
	where $u^*$ is the Schwarz rearrangement of $u$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By linearity, we can suppose $L=1$ and relabel $k(1)=\bar{k}=k$ and $\widetilde{F}_{j,1}=\widetilde{F}_j$. Assume preliminarily that each $\widetilde{F}_j$ is increasing. From \cite[Theorem 1.13]{LiebLoss} we have
	\[\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)\,dx & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\int_0^\infty\chi_{\{\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)>t_j\}}(x)\,dt_j\,dx\\
		& =\int_0^\infty\cdots\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\chi_{\{\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)>t_j\}}(x)\,dx\,dt_1\cdots \,dt_k
	\end{split}\]
	and similarly
	\[\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\widetilde{F}_j(u_j^*)\,dx & =\int_0^\infty\cdots\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\chi_{\{\widetilde{F}_j(u_j^*)>t_j\}}(x)\,dx\,dt_1\cdots \,dt_k\\
		& =\int_0^\infty\cdots\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\chi_{\{\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)>t_j\}^*}(x)\,dx\,dt_1\cdots \,dt_k
	\end{split}\]
	because
	\[
	\{\widetilde{F}_j(u_j^*)>t_j\}=\{u_j^*>\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t_j)\}=\{|u_j|>\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t_j)\}^*=\{\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)>t_j\}^*,
	\]
	therefore it suffices to prove that, for every $A_1,\dots,A_k\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ measurable with finite measure,
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\chi_{A_j}(x)\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\prod_{j=1}^k\chi_{A_j^*}(x)\,dx,
	\]
	i.e., $|\cap_{j=1}^kA_j|\le|\cap_{j=1}^kA_j^*|$.
	
	Up to relabelling the sets, we can assume that $|A_1|\le\cdots\le|A_k|$, whence $A_1^*\subset\cdots\subset A_k^*$ and so $|\cap_{j=1}^kA_j|\le|A_1|=|A_1^*|=|\cap_{j=1}^kA_j^*|$.
	
	Now assume that some $\widetilde{F}_j$'s are continuous with $\widetilde{F}_j(0)=0$. We want to prove that, as in the previous case, $\{\widetilde{F}_j(u_j^*)>t_j\}=\{\widetilde{F}_j(|u_j|)>t_j\}^*$.
	Since $\widetilde{F}_j\colon[0,\infty[\to[0,\infty[$ is nondecreasing and $\widetilde{F}_j(0)=0$, following, e.g., \cite[p. 10]{RaoRen} we can define the \textit{generalized inverse function} $\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}\colon[0,\infty[\to[0,\infty[$ as
	\[
	\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t):=\inf\{s>0:\widetilde{F}_j(s)>t\}.
	\]
	Then it suffices to prove that $\{\widetilde{F}_j(v)>t\}=\{v>\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t)\}$ for every $t>0$ and every measurable $v\colon\mathbb{R}^N\to[0,\infty[$ that vanishes at infinity. Observe that $\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t)=\infty$ if $t\ge\widetilde{F}_j\bigl(v(x)\bigr)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and, in that case, both sets above equal the empty set, hence we can assume that $t<\operatorname*{ess\,sup}\widetilde{F}_j\circ v$.
	
	Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ such that $\widetilde{F}_j\bigl(v(x)\bigr)>t$. Since $\widetilde{F}_j$ is continuous and $\widetilde{F}_j(0)=0$, there exists $s>0$ such that $t<\widetilde{F}_j(s)<\widetilde{F}_j\bigl(v(x)\bigr)$. Then $\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t)\le s$ and, since $\widetilde{F}_j$ is nondecreasing, $s<v(x)$. Now let $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ such that $v(x)>\widetilde{F}_j^{-1}(t)$. From the properties of infima, there exists $s>0$ such that $\widetilde{F}_j(s)>t$ and $v(x)\ge s$. Since $\widetilde{F}_j$ is nondecreasing, $\widetilde{F}_j\bigl(v(x)\bigr)\ge\widetilde{F}_j(s)$.

	\]
	Moreover, for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, either $u_j=0$ or $|u_j|_2=\rho_j$. In the latter case, $\lambda_j>0$ and $u_j$ is positive, radially nonincreasing, and of class $\mathcal{C}^2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of Proposition \ref{P:main2} we only need to prove that $u_j\ne0$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ (recall that $u_j=0$ if $\lambda_j=0$). Assume by contradiction that it does not hold. Up to changing the order, we can suppose that $u_K=0$. For every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ define
	\[
	J_j(w)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla w|^2-F_j(w)\,dx, \quad w\inH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)
	\]
	and
	\[
	\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}(j)=\Set{w\in\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}|\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}w^2\,dx\le\rho_j^2}.
	\]
	Of course, $-\Delta u_j+\lambda_ju_j=F_j'(u_j)$ and, from Lemmas \ref{L:cbb} and \ref{L:neg}, $-\infty<c_j:=\inf_{\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}(j)}J_j<0$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$. Moreover,
	\[
	J(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}J_j(u_j)\ge\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}c_j.
	\]
	Since $\widetilde{F}_{j,\ell}\ge0$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ and $\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}$, we have $J(w)\le\sum_{j=1}^KJ_j(w_j)$ for every $w=(w_1,\dots,w_K)\inH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$, thus
	\[
	\sum_{j=1}^Kc_j\ge\inf_{\mathfrak{D}_\textup{r}}J=J(u)\ge\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}c_j,
	\]
	whence $c_K\ge0$, a contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(i)} It is obvious from the definition of $m$.
	
	\textit{(ii)} Note preliminarily that, under these assumptions, for every $\rho\in\mathcal{A}$ there exists a minimizer of $J|_{\mathcal{D}(\rho)}$. Let $\rho^n,\rho\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $\rho^n\to \rho$ (note that $\mathcal{A}$ is open). Let $u^n\in\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$ such that $J(u^n)=m(\rho^n)\le m(\rho/2)$. Up to replacing $u^n$ with $(u^n)^*$, we can assume $u^n\in\mathfrak{H}_\textup{r}$. Since $u^n\in\mathcal{D}(2\rho)$, from Lemma \ref{L:cbb} and Remark \ref{R:cbb} there exists $u\in\mathcal{D}(\rho)$ such that $u^n\rightharpoonup u$ up to a subsequence, whence arguing as in Lemma \ref{L:min}
	\begin{equation}\label{e-cont1}
		m(\rho)\le J(u)\le \liminf_nJ(u^n)=\liminf_nm(\rho^n).
	\end{equation}
	Next, let $v\in\mathcal{D}(\rho)$ such that $J(v)=m(\rho)$ and define $v^n:=(\rho^n_jv_j/\rho_j)_{j=1}^K\in\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$. Then $v^n\to v$ and so
	\begin{equation}\label{e-cont2}
		m(\rho)=J(v)=\lim_nJ(v^n)\ge\limsup_nm(\rho^n).
	\end{equation}
	The continuity of $m$ follows from \eqref{e-cont1} and \eqref{e-cont2}.
	
	\textit{(iii)} Note that \eqref{e-etas} holds for every sufficiently small $\rho$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Let $\mathcal{A}\ni \rho^n\to0$ and $u^n\in\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$ such that $J(u^n)\le m(\rho^n)+\varepsilon$. In particular, $u^n\to0$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ and $u^n\in\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\rho})$ for some $\tilde{\rho}\in]0,\infty[^K$, therefore $u^n$ is bounded in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ due to Lemma \ref{L:cbb} and Remark \ref{R:cbb}. This, together with (F1), (F2), and Theorem \ref{T:GN}, yields $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(u^n)\,dx\to0$, which implies $\liminf_nJ(u^n)=\liminf_n|\nabla u^n|_2^2/2\ge0$,
    
                                                                                         
    
	whence, in view also of Lemma \ref{L:neg} and Remark \ref{R:neg}, $0\ge\limsup_nm(\rho^n)\ge\liminf_nm(\rho^n)\ge-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\to0^+$ we conclude.
	
	\textit{(iv)} Note that \eqref{e-etal} holds for every sufficiently large $\rho$. Fix $\rho\in\mathcal{A}$, $u\in\mathcal{D}(\rho)\setminus\{0\}$ and note that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(u)\,dx>0$ from (F3). For every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ let $\rho_j^n\to\infty$ and denote $a_n:=\max_{j=1,\dots,K}\rho_j/\rho_j^n$ and $u^n(x):=u(a_n^{2/N}x)$. Then $\lim_na_n=0$, $u^n\in\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$, and
	\[
	m(\rho^n)\le J(u^n)=\frac1{a_n^2}\left(a_n^{4/N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla u|^2\,dx-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(u)\,dx\right)\to-\infty.
	\]
	
	\textit{(v)} Let $\rho,\bar{\rho}\in\mathcal{A}$ as in the statement. Clearly $m(\rho)\ge m(\bar{\rho})$ from item \textit{(i)}. If $m(\rho)=m(\bar{\rho})$, then there exists $u\in\mathcal{S}(\rho)\subset\mathcal{D}(\bar{\rho})\setminus\mathcal{S}(\bar{\rho})$ such that $J(u)=m(\rho)=m(\bar{\rho})$, which is impossible. The same argument applies to the version of item \textit{(v)} that involves minimizers with nonnegative components.

title: Proof
body_md:
From Theorem \ref{T:GN}, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $c_\varepsilon$ such that for every $u\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$
	\[\begin{split}
		|\nabla u|_2^2&=\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} H(u)\,dx\le 2^*\bigl(c_\varepsilon|u|_{2^*}^{2^*}+(\varepsilon+\eta)|u|_{2_\#}^{2_\#}\bigr)\\
		&=2^*\left(c_\varepsilon\big||u|\big|_{2^*}^{2^*}+(\varepsilon+\eta)\big||u|\big|_{2_\#}^{2_\#}\right)\\
		&\le2^*\left(c_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*}\big|\nabla|u|\big|_2^{2^*}+(\varepsilon+\eta)C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}\big|\nabla|u|\big|_2^2\right)\\
		&\le2^*\bigl(c_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*}|\nabla u|_2^{2^*}+(\varepsilon+\eta)C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}|\nabla u|_2^2\bigr)
	\end{split}\]
	i.e.
	\[
	0\le2^*c_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*}|\nabla u|_2^{2^*}+\bigl(2^*(\varepsilon+\eta)C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}-1\bigr)|\nabla u|_2^2
	\]
	Taking $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small so that
	\[
	2^*(\varepsilon+\eta)C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}<1
	\]
	we conclude.
head: environment

label: L:phi
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice that from (F1)
	\[
	\varphi(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{s^2}{2}|\nabla u|^2-\frac{F(s^{N/2}u)}{s^N}\,dx\to0
	\]
	as $s\to0^+$, while from (F2) $\lim_{s\to\infty}\varphi(s)=-\infty$.
	From (F1) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $c_\varepsilon>0$ such that
	\[
	F(u)\le(\varepsilon+\eta)|u|^{2_\#}+c_\varepsilon|u|^{2^*},
	\]
	therefore,
	\[
	\varphi(s)\geq s^2\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1}{2}|\nabla u|^2-(\eta+\varepsilon)|u|^{2_\#}\,dx\Big)-c_\varepsilon s^{2^*}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^{2^*}\,dx>0
	\]
	for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ and $s$.	
	It follows that there exists an interval $[a,b]\subset]0,\infty[$ such that $\varphi|_{[a,b]}=\max\varphi$. Moreover
	\[
	\varphi'(s)=s\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2-\frac{N}{2}\frac{H(s^{N/2}u)}{s^{N+2}}\,dx
	\]
	and the function
	\[
	s\in]0,\infty[\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{H(s^{N/2}u)}{s^{N+2}}\,dx
	\]
	is nondecreasing (resp. increasing) due to (F4) (resp. (F4,$\preceq$) and Lemma \ref{L:ineq}) and tends to $\infty$ as $s\to\infty$ due to (F2) and (F5). There follows that $\varphi'(s)>0$ if $s\in(0,a)$ and $\varphi'(s)<0$ if $s>b$ and that $a=b$ if (F4,$\preceq$) holds. Finally, observe that
	\[
	s\varphi'(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}s^2|\nabla u|^2-\frac{N}{2}\frac{H(s^{N/2}u)}{s^N}\,dx=M(s\star u).\qedhere
	\]
head: environment

label: L:coerc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:coerc}
	If (F0)--(F2), (F4), (F5), and \eqref{e-eta2} are verified, then $J$ is coercive on $\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First of all, note that, if $u\in\mathcal{M}$, then due to (F5)
	\[
	J(u)=J(u)-\frac12M(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(u)-F(u)\,dx\ge0
	\]
	and so, a fortiori, $J$ is nonegative on $\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$.
	Let $u^n\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$ such that $\|u^n\|\to\infty$, i.e., $\lim_n|\nabla u^n|_2=\infty$, and define
	\[
	s_n:=|\nabla u^n|_2^{-1}>0\quad\text{and}\quad w^n:=s_n\star u^n.
	\]
	Note that $s_n\to0$, $|w^n_j|_2=|u^n_j|_2\le\rho_j$ for $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, and $|\nabla w^n|_2=1$, in particular $w^n$ is bounded in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$.
	Suppose by contradiction that
	\[
	\limsup_n\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^N}\int_{B(y,1)}|w^n|^2\,dx>0.
	\]
	Then there exist $y^n\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and $w\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ such that, up to a subsequence, $w^n(\cdot+y^n)\rightharpoonup w\ne0$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ and $w^n(\cdot+y^n)\to w$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Thus, owing to (F2),
	\[\begin{split}
		0&\le\frac{J(u^n)}{|\nabla u^n|_2^2}=\frac12-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(u^n)}{|\nabla u^n|_2^2}\,dx=\frac12-s_n^{N+2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F\bigl(u^n(s_nx)\bigr)\,dx\\
		&=\frac12-s_n^{N+2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(s_n^{-N/2}w^n)=\frac12-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(s_n^{-N/2}w^n)}{|s_n^{-N/2}w^n|^{2_\#}}|w^n|^{2_\#}\,dx\\
		&=\frac12-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F\bigl(s_n^{-N/2}w^n(x+y^n)\bigr)}{|s_n^{-N/2}w^n(x+y^n)|^{2_\#}}|w^n(x+y^n)|^{2_\#}\,dx\to-\infty.
	\end{split}\]
	It follows that
	\[
	\lim_n\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^N}\int_{B(y,1)}|w^n|^2\,dx=0
	\]
	and so, from \cite[Lemma I.1]{Lions84_2}, $w^n\to0$ in $L^{2_\#}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$. Since
	\[
	s_n^{-1}\star w^n=u^n\in\mathcal{M},
	\]
	Lemma \ref{L:phi} yields
	\[
	J(u^n)=J(s_n^{-1}\star w^n)\ge J(s\star w^n)=\frac{s^2}{2}-s^N\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(s^{N/2}w^n)\,dx
	\]
	for every $s>0$. Taking into account that
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(s^{N/2}w^n)\,dx=0,
	\]
	we have that $\liminf_nJ(u^n)\ge s^2/2$ for every $s>0$, i.e., $\lim_nJ(u^n)=\infty$.
head: environment

label: L:bdaw2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:bdaw2}
	If (F0)--(F2), (F4), (F5), and \eqref{e-eta2} are verified, then $\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J>0$.
head: environment

label: e-alpha
title: Proof
body_md:
We prove that there exists $\alpha>0$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-alpha}
		|\nabla u|_2\le\alpha\Rightarrow J(u)\ge\frac{|\nabla u|_2^2}{2N}.
	\end{equation}
	From Theorem \ref{T:GN} and \eqref{e-eta2}, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $c_\varepsilon>0$ such that
	\[\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(u)\,dx&\le c_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*}|\nabla u|_2^{2^*}+(\varepsilon+\eta)C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}|\nabla u|_2^2\\
		&\le\left(c_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*}|\nabla u|_2^{2^*-2}+\varepsilon C_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}+\frac12-\frac1N\right)|\nabla u|_2^2.
	\end{split}\]
	Choosing
	\[
	\varepsilon=\frac{1}{4NC_{N,2_\#}^{2_\#}|\rho|^{4/N}} \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha=\frac{1}{(4Nc_\varepsilon C_{N,2^*}^{2^*})^\frac{1}{2^*-2}}
	\]
	we obtain, provided $|\nabla u|_2\le\alpha$,
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(u)\,dx\le\biggl(\frac12-\frac{1}{2N}\biggr)|\nabla u|_2^2
	\]
	and so $\displaystyle J(u)\ge\frac{|\nabla u|_2^2}{2N}$.
	Now take $u\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$ and $\alpha>0$ such that \eqref{e-alpha} holds and define
	\[
	s:=\frac{\alpha}{|\nabla u|_2}\quad\text{and}\quad w:=s\star u.
	\]
	Clearly $|w_j|_2=|u_j|_2\le\rho_j$ for $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ and $|\nabla w|_2=\alpha$, whence in view of Lemma \ref{L:phi}
	\[
	J(u)\ge J(w)\ge\frac{|\nabla w|_2^2}{2N}=\frac{\alpha^2}{2N}>0.\qedhere
	\]

label: L:infismin
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:infismin}
	If (F0)--(F5) and \eqref{e-eta2} hold, then $\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$ is attained.
head: environment

label: eq:claim1
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u^n\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$ such that $\lim_nJ(u^n)=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$. Then $u^n$ is bounded due to Lemma \ref{L:coerc} and, in view of Lemma \ref{L:split}, we find $(\tilde{u}^i)_{i=0}^\infty\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ and $(y_n^{i,n})_{i=0}^\infty\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ such that \eqref{eq:Me1}--\eqref{eq:Me3} hold. Let
	\[
	I:=\{i\ge0:\tilde{u}^i\ne0\}
	\]
	and suppose by contradiction that $I=\emptyset$. Then, since $u^n\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$, there holds
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u^n|\,dx=\lim_n\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(u^n)\,dx=0
	\]
	owing to \eqref{eq:Me3}, which contradicts Lemma \ref{L:bdaw1}. Now we prove that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:claim1}
		\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(\tilde{u}^i)\,dx\ge\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla\tilde{u}^i|^2\,dx
	\end{equation}
	for some $i\in I$. Assume by contradiction that
	\[
	\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(\tilde{u}^i)\,dx<\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla\tilde{u}^i|^2\,dx
	\]
	for every $i\in I$. Then from \eqref{eq:Me2} and \eqref{eq:Me3} we have
	\[\begin{split}
		\limsup_n\,\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(u^n)\,dx=\limsup_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u^n|^2\ge\sum_{i=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla\tilde{u}^i|^2\\
		>\sum_{i=0}^\infty\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(\tilde{u}^i)\,dx=\limsup_n\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(u^n)\,dx,
	\end{split}\]
	a contradiction. Let $\tilde u=\tilde{u}^i$ satisfy \eqref{eq:claim1} for some $i\in I$. Then there exists $R>0$ such that $\tilde u(R\cdot)\in\mathcal{M}$ and again from \eqref{eq:claim1} we indeed know that $R\geq 1$, whence $\tilde{u}(R\cdot)\in\mathcal{D}$. Hence Fatou's Lemma yields
	\[\begin{split}
		\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J&\le J\bigl(\tilde u(R\cdot)\bigr)=J\bigl(\tilde u(R\cdot)\bigr)-\frac12M\bigl(\tilde u(R\cdot)\bigr)\,dx\\
		&=\frac{1}{R^N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(\tilde u)-F(\tilde{u})\,dx\le\liminf_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(u^n)-F(u^n)\,dx\\
		&=\liminf_nJ(u^n)-\frac12M(u^n)=\liminf_nJ(u^n)=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J,
	\end{split}\]
	i.e., $R=1$ and $J(\tilde{u})=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$.
head: environment

label: L:radmin
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tilde{u}\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$ such that $J(\tilde{u})=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$ be given by Lemma \ref{L:infismin}.
	For simplicity, let us denote, for every $j=1,\dots,K$, $u_j:=\tilde{u}_j^*$ and $u:=(u_1,\dots,u_K)$. Let $a=a(u)$ be determined by Lemma \ref{L:phi}. Since
	\[
	M(1\star u)=M(u)\le M(\tilde{u})=0,
	\]
	in view of Lemma \ref{L:phi} we have that $a\le1$ and, consequently, $M(a\star\tilde{u})\ge0$. Let
	\[
	d:=\frac{N}{2}\max_{\ell=1,\dots, L}\left(\sum_{j=1}^Kr_{j,\ell}-2\right)\ge2.
	\]
	Then, from Lemma \ref{L:Schwarz},
	\[\begin{split}
		\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J\le \, & J(a\star u)=J(a\star u)-\frac{1}{d}M(a\star u)\\
		= \, &\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\sum_{j=1}^Ka^2\biggl(\frac12-\frac{1}{d}\biggr)|\nabla u_i|^2+\frac{1}{a^N}\biggl(\frac{N}{2d}H_j(a^{N/2}u_j)-F_j(a^{N/2}u_j)\biggr)\,dx\\
		&-\frac{1}{a^N}
		\sum_{\ell=1}^L\beta_\ell\Bigg(1-\frac1{d}\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^Kr_{j,\ell}-2\bigg)\Bigg)\prod_{j=1}^K|a^{N/2}u_j|^{r_{j,\ell}}\\
		\le \, &\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\sum_{j=1}^Ka^2\biggl(\frac12-\frac{1}{d}\biggr)|\nabla\tilde{u}_j|^2+\frac{1}{a^N}\biggl(\frac{N}{2d}H_j(a^{N/2}\tilde{u}_j)-F_j(a^{N/2}\tilde{u}_j)\biggr)\,dx\\
		&-\frac{1}{a^N}
		\sum_{\ell=1}^L\beta_\ell\Bigg(1-\frac1{d}\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^Kr_{j,\ell}-2\bigg)\Bigg)\prod_{j=1}^K|a^{N/2}\tilde{u}_j|^{r_{j,\ell}}\\
		= \, &J(a\star\tilde{u})-\frac{1}{d}M(a\star\tilde{u})\le J(a\star\tilde{u})\le J(\tilde{u})=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J,
	\end{split}\]
	i.e., $J(a\star u)=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$.
head: environment

label: L:minons
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: e-solution
title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{(a)} 
	In Proposition \ref{P:Clarke} we put $m=K$, $n=1$, $\mathcal{H}=H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$, $f=J$,  $\phi_j=|\cdot|_2^2-\rho_j^2$ for all $1\leq j\leq K$, and $\psi_1=M$. Then there exist $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K)\in[0,\infty[^K$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-solution}
	-(1-2\sigma)\Delta u_j+\lambda_ju_j=\partial_jF(u)-\sigma\frac{N}{2}\partial_jH(u)
	\end{equation}
	for every $i\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ and $u$ satisfies the Nehari identity
	\begin{equation}\label{e-sigN}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(1-2\sigma)|\nabla u|^2+\sum_{j=1}^K\lambda_ju_j^2+\sigma\frac{N}{2}h(u)\cdot u-f(u)\cdot u\,dx=0.
	\end{equation}
	If $\sigma=1/2$, then (F4,$\preceq$), (F5), and \eqref{e-sigN} yield
	\[\begin{split}
	0&\ge\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}h(u)\cdot u-f(u)\cdot u\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}h(u)\cdot u-H(u)-2F(u)\,dx\\
	&>\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{2}H(u)-2F(u)\,dx\ge0,
	\end{split}\]
	a contradiction. Hence $\sigma\ne1/2$ and $u$ satisfies also the Poho\v{z}aev identity
	\begin{equation}\label{e-sigP}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(1-2\sigma)|\nabla u|^2+\frac{2^*}{2}\sum_{j=1}^K\lambda_ju_j^2+2^*\left(\sigma\frac{N}{2}H(u)-F(u)\right)\,dx=0.
	\end{equation}
	Combining \eqref{e-sigN} and  \eqref{e-sigP} we obtain
	\[
	(1-2\sigma)\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2\,dx+\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\sigma N\left(\frac12h(u)\cdot u-H(u)\right)-H(u)\,dx=0
	\]
	and, using the fact that $u\in\mathcal{M}$,
	\[
	(1-2\sigma)\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}H(u)\,dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\sigma N\left(\frac12h(u)\cdot u-H(u)\right)-H(u)\,dx=0,
	\]
	that is,
	\[
	\sigma\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}h(u)\cdot u-2_\#H(u)\,dx=0,
	\]
	which together with (F4,$\preceq$) yields $\sigma=0$. Since $u\in W^{2,p}_\textup{loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ for all $p < \infty$, we can argue as in the proof of \cite[Lemma 1]{BerLions} and have that $u$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^2$.
	
	\textit{(b)} Suppose by contradiction that $\lambda_1=\dots=\lambda_K=0$, which is the case when $|u_j|<\rho_j$ for every $j$. From \eqref{e-sigN} and \eqref{e-sigP} (with $\sigma=0$) there follows
	\begin{equation}\label{e-Gg2^*}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(u)\cdot u-2^*F(u)\,dx=0.
	\end{equation}
	In view of (F5) 
	\begin{equation}\label{e-pointSob}
	2^*F\bigl(u(x)\bigr)=f\bigl(u(x)\bigr)\cdot u(x)
	\end{equation}
	for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Since $F_j$ satisfies the scalar variant of (F5), $2^*F_j\bigl(u_j(x)\bigr)\geq f_j\bigl(u_j(x)\bigr)u_j(x)$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ and note that
	\[
	2^*\sum_{\ell=1}^L\beta_\ell\prod_{j=1}^K|u_j(x)|^{r_{j,\ell}}\geq \sum_{\ell=1}^L\beta_\ell\sum_{k=1}^K r_{k,\ell}\prod_{j=1}^K|u_j(x)|^{r_{j,\ell}},
	\]
	hence, from \eqref{e-pointSob}, the equalities above are actually equalities. On the other hand, for every $\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}$, $\sum_{j=1}^Kr_{j,\ell}<2^*$, which yields $\beta_\ell=0$ or $\prod_{j=1}^K|u_j(x)|^{r_{j,\ell}}=0$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, thus
	$$2^* F_j\bigl(u_j(x)\bigr)=f_j\bigl(u_j(x)\bigr)u_j(x)$$
	for every $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ and every $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
	
	Now fix $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ such that $u_j\neq 0$. Since $u_j\inH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, there exists an open interval $I\subset \mathbb{R}$ such that $0 \in\overline{I}$ and $2^*F_j(s)=f_j(s)s$ for $s\in\overline{I}$. Then $F_j(s)=c|s|^{2^*}$ for some $c>0$, $s\in \overline{I}$, and $u_j\ge0$ solves $-\Delta u_j=2^*c|u_j|^{2^*-2}u_j$. Hence $u_j$ is an Aubin--Talenti instanton, up to scaling and translations, which is not $L^2$-integrable because $N\in\{3,4\}$, see \cite{Aubin_fr,Talenti}. 
	
	Suppose that there exists $\nu\in\{1,\dots,K-1\}$ such that, up to changing the order, $|u_j|_2<\rho_j$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,\nu\}$ and $|u_j|_2=\rho_j$ for every $j\in\{\nu+1,\dots,K\}$.
	Arguing as before, there exist $0=\lambda_1=\dots=\lambda_{\nu}\leq \lambda_{\nu+1},\dots,\lambda_K$ such that
	\begin{equation*}                 
	\begin{cases}
	-\Delta u_j=\partial_jF(u), \quad j\in\{1,\dots,\nu\}\\
	-\Delta u_j+\lambda_ju_j=\partial_jF(u), \quad j\in\{\nu+1,\dots,K\}.
	\end{cases}
	\end{equation*}
	Since $F_j$ satisfies the scalar variant of (F5), $s\in]0,\infty[\mapsto F_j(s)/s^{2_\#}\in\mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing, hence
	$F_j$ is nondecreasing as well for all $j$. Then, the first $\nu$ equations in the system above yield $-\Delta u_j\ge0$ for $j\in\{1,\dots,\nu\}$. Since  $u\in L^{\frac{N}{N-2}}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ as $N\in\{3,4\}$, \cite[Lemma A.2]{Ikoma} implies $u_j=0$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,\nu\}$. Notice we have proved that $\lambda_j=0$ implies $u_j=0$, hence, in particular, $\lambda_j>0$ for every $j\in\{\nu+1,\dots,K\}$.

label: R:alt
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R:alt}
We point out that, if (F0)--(F3), (F4,$\preceq$), (F5), and \eqref{e-eta2} hold, $u\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}$, and $J(u)=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$, then we can show that $u\in\partial\mathcal{D}$ for any dimension $N\geq 3$ provided that $H\preceq(2^*-2)F$ holds. As a matter of fact, observe that \eqref{e-Gg2^*} contradicts $H\preceq(2^*-2)F$  and Lemma \ref{L:ineq}. This gives a somewhat alternative proof of Lemma \ref{L:minons} \textit{(b)}.

\label{L:minons2}
	Suppose that $K=2$, $L=1$ and the assumptions in Lemma \ref{L:minons} \textit{(b)} hold. If $r_{1,1}+r_{2,1}>2_\#$ and $\beta_1$ is sufficiently large, then $u\in\mathcal{S}$.

label: e-sup
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $L=1$, we denote $\beta_1$, $r_{1,1}$, $r_{2,1}$ by  $\beta$, $r_{1}$, $r_{2}$ respectively.
	Suppose by contradiction that $u_1=0$ or $u_2=0$, say $u_1=0$, which implies that $|u_2|_2=\rho_2$. We want to find a suitable $w\in\mathcal{S}$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-sup}
		J(a\star w)<\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J,           
	\end{equation}
	where $a=a(w)$ is defined in Lemma \ref{L:phi} (note that $a(w)=b(w)$ because (F4,$\preceq$) holds), which is impossible.
	First we show that $\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J$ does not depend on $\beta$. Consider the functional
	\[
	J_*\colon v\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac12|\nabla v|^2-F_2(v)\,dx\in\mathbb{R}
	\]
	and the sets
	\[\begin{split}
		\mathcal{D}_* & := \Set{ v \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N) | \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} v^2 \, dx \leq \rho_2^2 },\\
		\mathcal{M}_* & := \Set{ v \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N) \setminus \{0\} | \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla v|^2 \, dx = \frac{N}2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} H_2(v) }.
	\end{split}\]
	Observe that $J(0,v)=J_*(v)$ for $v\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.  Moreover, $(0,v)\in\mathcal{D}$ if and only if $v\in\mathcal{D}_*$, and $(0,v)\in\mathcal{M}$ if and only if $v\in\mathcal{M}_*$. In particular,
	\[\begin{split}
	\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J&=J(0,u_2)=J_*(u_2)\ge\inf_{\mathcal{M}_*\cap\mathcal{D}_*}J_*\\
	&=\inf\Set{J(0,v)|(0,v)\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}\ge\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J,
	\end{split}\]
	i.e., $\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J=\inf_{\mathcal{M}_*\cap\mathcal{D}_*}J_*$, and the claim follows because $J_*$, $\mathcal{D}_*$, and $\mathcal{M}_*$ do not depend on $\beta$.
	
	In view of Theorem \ref{T:Main2} for $K=1$, there exists $\bar{v}\in\mathcal{M}_*\cap\partial\mathcal{D}_*$ such that $$J_*(\bar{v})=\inf_{\mathcal{M}_*\cap\mathcal{D}_*}J_*=\inf_{\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}}J=\inf_{\mathcal{M}_*\cap\partial\mathcal{D}_*}J_*.$$ Note that $\bar{v}$ does not depend on $\beta$. Define $w=(w_1,w_2):=\bigl(\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}\bar{v},\bar{v}\bigr)$.
	From Lemma \ref{L:phi}, $a=a_\beta$ is implicitly defined by
	\[\begin{split}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla w|^2\,dx=&\,\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F_1'(a_\beta^{N/2}w_1)a_\beta^{N/2}w_1-2F_1(a_\beta^{N/2}w_1)}{a_\beta^{N+2}}\\
		&+\frac{F_2'(a_\beta^{N/2}w_2)a_\beta^{N/2}w_2-2F_2(a_\beta^{N/2}w_2)}{a_\beta^{N+2}}\\
		&+\beta(r_1+r_2-2)a_\beta^{N(r_1+r_2-2)/2-2}w_1^{r_1}w_2^{r_2}\,dx\\
		\ge&\,\beta(r_1+r_2-2)a_\beta^{N(r_1+r_2-2)/2-2}\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} w_1^{r_1}w_2^{r_2}\,dx,
	\end{split}\]
	hence there exist $C>0$ not depending on $\beta$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-beta1}
		0<\beta a_\beta^{N(r_1+r_2-2)/2-2}\le C,
	\end{equation}
	whence
	\begin{equation}\label{e-beta2}
		\lim_{\beta\to\infty}a_\beta=0.
	\end{equation}
	Since $a_\beta\star w\in\mathcal{M}$, we have from (F5)
	\[\begin{split}
		J(a_\beta\star w)=&\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(a_\beta\star w)-F(a_\beta\star w)\,dx\le\frac{2}{N-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} F(a_\beta\star w)\,dx\\
		=&\,\frac{2}{N-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F_1(a_\beta^{N/2}w_1)+F_2(a_\beta^{N/2}w_2)}{a_\beta^N}\,dx\\
		&+\frac{2\beta a_\beta^{N(r_1+r_2-2)/2}}{N-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} w_1^{r_1}w_2^{r_2}\,dx,
	\end{split}\]
	therefore \eqref{e-sup} holds true for sufficiently large $\beta$ owing to (F1), \eqref{e-beta1}, and \eqref{e-beta2}.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P:GSE}
	Assume that (F0) is satisfied and let $\mathcal{A}$ be the subset of $]0,\infty[^K$ where \eqref{e-eta2} holds. Then $m\colon]0,\infty[^K\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ is nonincreasing and. If (F0)--(F5) are satisfied, then $m|_\mathcal{A}$ is continuous and
	\[
	\lim_{|\rho|\to0^+}m(\rho)=\infty.
	\]
	If (F0)--(F5) are satisfied and every ground state solution to \eqref{e-mainineq} belongs to $\mathcal{S}(\rho)$ (e.g., if the assumptions of Theorem \ref{T:Main3} are satisfied), then $m|_\mathcal{A}$ is decreasing.

label: e-conts
title: Proof
body_md:
The monotonicity of $m$ is obvious. Fix $\rho\in\mathcal{A}$ and let $\mathcal{A}\ni\rho^n\to\rho$ (note that $\mathcal{A}$ is open). Let $u^n\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)\subset\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}(2\rho)$ such that $J(u^n)=m(\rho^n)\le m(\rho/2)$. In view of Lemma \ref{L:coerc}, $u^n$ is bounded and so, arguing as in Lemma \ref{L:infismin}, there exists $u\in\mathcal{D}(\rho)\setminus\{0\}$ such that, up to subsequences and translations, $u^n\rightharpoonup u$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$, $u^n\to u$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$, and $R\ge1$, where $R=R_u>0$ is such that $u(R\cdot)\in\mathcal{M}$. Fatou's Lemma and (F4) yield
	\[\begin{split}
	m(\rho)&\le J\bigl(u(R\cdot)\bigr)=\frac{1}{R^N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(u)-F(u)\,dx\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{N}{4}H(u)-F(u)\,dx\\
	&\le\liminf_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{N}{4}H(u^n)-F(u^n)\,dx=\liminf_nJ(u^n)=\liminf_nm(\rho^n).
	\end{split}\]
	Now let $w\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}(\rho)$ such that $J(w)=m(\rho)$. Denote $w_i^n:=\rho_i^nw_i/\rho_i$ and consider $w^n=(w_1^n,\dots,w_K^n)\in\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$. Due to Lemma \ref{L:phi}, for every $n$ there exists $s_n>0$ such that $s_n\star w^n\in\mathcal{M}$. Note that
	\begin{equation}\label{e-conts}
	\begin{split}
	\frac{N}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{H\bigl(s_n^{N/2}(\rho_1^nw_1/\rho_1,\dots,\rho_K^nw_K/\rho_K)\bigr)}{s_n^{N+2}}\,dx\\
	=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla w^n|^2\,dx\to \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla w|^2\,dx.
	\end{split}
	\end{equation}
	If $\limsup_ns_n=\infty$, then from (F2) and (F5) the left-hand side of \eqref{e-conts} tends to $\infty$ up to a subsequence, which is a contradiction. If $\liminf_ns_n=0$, then from (F1), (F3), (F5) and \eqref{e-eta2} and arguing as in Lemma \ref{L:bdaw1} we obtain that the limit superior of the left-hand side of \eqref{e-conts} is less than $|\nabla w|_2^2$, which is again a contradiction. There follows that, up to a subsequence, $s_n\to s$ for some $s>0$ and $s\star w\in\mathcal{M}$. In view of Lemma \ref{L:phi},
	\[
	\limsup_nm(\rho^n)\le\lim_nJ(s_n\star w_n)=J(s\star w)=J(w)=m(\rho)
	\]
	and the continuity of $m|_\mathcal{A}$ is proved.
	
	Let $\rho^n\to0^+$ and $u^n\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{D}(\rho^n)$ such that $J(u^n)=m(\rho^n)$. Denote $s_n:=|\nabla u^n|_2^{-1}$ and $w^n:=s_n\star u^n$ and note that $s_n^{-1}\star w^n=u^n\in\mathcal{M}$, $|\nabla w^n|_2=1$ and
	\[
	|w^n|_2^2=|u^n|_2^2=|\rho^n|^2\to0
	\]
	as $n\to\infty$. In particular $w^n$ is bounded in $L^{2^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)^K$ and so
	\[
	|w^n|_{2_\#}\le|w^n|_2^\frac{2}{N+2}|w^n|_{2^*}^\frac{N}{N+2}\to0
	\]
	as $n\to\infty$. Then, in view of (F1) and (F3), for every $s>0$
	\[
	\lim_n\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(s^{N/2}w^n)}{s^{-N}}\,dx=0
	\]
	and, consequently,
	\[
	J(u^n)=J(s_n^{-1}\star w^n)\ge J(s\star w^n)=\frac{s^2}{2}-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{F(s^{N/2}w^n)}{s^{-N}}\,dx=\frac{s^2}{2}+o(1),
	\]
	whence $\lim_nJ(u^n)=\infty$.
	
	The last part is proved similarly to Proposition \ref{P:gsem} \textit{(v)}.

label: e-NehSing
title: Remark
body_md:
The set $\mathcal{Q}$ is obtained as the counterpart of $\mathcal{M}$ for the problem \eqref{e-normsing}. Nonetheless, one can obtain it directly from the Nehari and Poho\v{z}aev identities corresponding to \eqref{e-normsing}. As a matter of fact, arguing as in Section \ref{S:NP}, if $(\lambda,u)$ is such that
\[
-\Delta u+\frac{u}{|y|^2}+\lambda u=f(u) \quad \text{in } \mathbb{R}^N,
\]
then it clearly satisfies the Nehari identity
\begin{equation}\label{e-NehSing}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2+\frac{u^2}{|y|^2}+\lambda u^2\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(u)u\,dx.
\end{equation}
In addition, if $u\in W_\textup{loc}^{2,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for every $p<\infty$ (or, in general, arguing heuristically), then $1$ is a critical point of the functional
\[
t\in]0,\infty[\mapsto J\bigl(u(t\cdot)\bigr)+\frac{\lambda}2\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u^2(tx)\,dx\in\mathbb{R},
\]
i.e., after explicit computations,
\begin{equation}\label{e-PohSing}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(N-2)\left(|\nabla u|^2+\frac{u^2}{|y|^2}\right)+\lambda Nu^2-2NF(u)\,dx.
\end{equation}

Finally, as in Section \ref{S:prel}, combining linearly \eqref{e-NehSing} and \eqref{e-PohSing}, we obtain
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2+\frac{u^2}{|y|^2}-\frac{N}2f(u)u+NF(u)\,dx=0.
\]

body_md: We prove as in Lemma \ref{L:cbb} (see also Remark \ref{R:cbb}) that $E|_{D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*}$ is coercive (and bounded from below) and consider a minimizing sequence $\mathbf{U}_n\in D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*$ for $E|_{D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*}$, which is therefore bounded and, up to a subsequence, $\mathbf{U}_n\rightharpoonup\mathbf{U}$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N,\mathbb{R}^N)$ for some $\mathbf{U}\in D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*$. Then, as in Lemma \ref{L:min}, we have that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}G(\mathbf{U}_n)\,dx\to\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}G(\mathbf{U})\,dx$ and so $E(\mathbf{U})=\inf_{D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*}E$. Moreover, as in Lemma \ref{L:neg}, $E(s\star\mathbf{V})<0$ for $\mathbf{V}\in D_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*\setminus\{0\}$ and $0<s\ll1$, thus $E(\mathbf{U})<0$. Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{T:main1}, there exists $\lambda\ge0$ such that $\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{U}+\lambda\mathbf{U}=g(\mathbf{U})$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and, if $\lambda=0$, then $E(\mathbf{U})\ge0$, hence $\lambda>0$ and, consequently, $\mathbf{U}\in S_\mathcal{F}\cap\mathfrak{H}_\textup{s}^*$, i.e., $(\lambda,\mathbf{U})$ is a solution to \eqref{e-normcurl}.

body_md:
Assume $f$ and $g$ are as in Proposition \ref{P:equiv} and let $(\lambda,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times H_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{O}}$ be a solution to \eqref{e-normsing}. If we define $\mathbf{U}$ from $u$ using \eqref{e-uU}, then, in virtue of Theorem \ref{T:equiv} and Lemma \ref{L:DivFree} respectively, $(\lambda,\mathbf{U})\in\mathbb{R}\times H_\mathcal{F}$ is a solution to \eqref{e-normcurl} and $\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{U}=-\Delta\mathbf{U}$. Consequently, $(\lambda,\mathbf{U})$ satisfies the Poho\v{z}aev identity (corresponding to \eqref{e-normcurl})
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla\times\mathbf{U}|^2\,dx=\frac{N}{N-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}2G(\mathbf{U})-\lambda|\mathbf{U}|^2\,dx
\]
and so, again from the same arguments as in Theorem \ref{T:equiv}, $(\lambda,u)$ satisfies \eqref{e-PohSing}. This last property is definitely not trivial because, due to the singular term $u/|y|^2$, a solution $\tilde{u}\inH^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\cap X$ to the differential equation in \eqref{e-normsing} (for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{R})$ need not belong to $W_\textup{loc}^{2,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for every $p<\infty$.
